subject: rla
title: Grammar I: Sentence Structure
objectives: You will tell complete sentences from fragments and fix fragments by attaching them to a nearby sentence or adding a missing subject or verb.
You will recognize run-ons and comma splices and fix them five ways: a period, a semicolon, a comma with a FANBOYS word, a semicolon with a transition, or a subordinating word.
You will join ideas with coordination, subordination, and transitions that match the logical relationship, and punctuate them correctly.
You will find and fix misplaced and dangling modifiers so every describing phrase points to the right word.
You will revise lists and paired ideas for parallel structure in GED-style editing items.

slides.title: Grammar I: Sentence Structure
slides.board:
Week 7 · Reasoning Through Language Arts

Today you will:

  • Tell complete sentences from fragments, and fix fragments
  • Fix run-ons and comma splices five ways
  • Join ideas with the right word for the logic
  • Fix misplaced and dangling modifiers
  • Keep lists and pairs parallel

Plan: Warm-up · Learn and practice together · Your turn · GED questions · Recap

notes.say: Today we start the language strand of the RLA test. On the GED, these are the drop-down questions inside short drafts: an email, a memo, a notice, a letter. A menu sits in the middle of a sentence and you pick the version that makes it correct and clear. You do not need to memorize grammar terms to do well. You need to notice when a sentence is broken and know a few reliable repairs. That is exactly what we will build this hour. Next week covers the rest of the language skills: agreement, pronouns, tense, confused words, capitalization, and punctuation.
ask: When you write an email for work, what do you check before you hit send? (expected: any honest answer; build on spelling, tone, or “whether it makes sense”)

slides.title: Warm-up: two texts, one topic
slides.board:
Passage 1 (a resident's letter): Gas leaf blowers should be banned in Millbrook. The noise wakes my baby every Saturday morning, and everyone I know hates them.

Passage 2 (a landscaper's column): A sudden ban would hurt small landscaping businesses. Battery blowers cost about twice as much, and many batteries last under an hour. The town should phase in a ban over three years and offer rebates.

  1. What is each writer's claim?
  2. Who is speaking in each passage?
  3. Whose evidence is stronger? Why?
  4. Passage 2 vs. Passage 1: agree, disagree, add, or complicate?
steps: 1. Passage 1: ban gas leaf blowers now. Passage 2: a sudden ban hurts small businesses, so phase it in over three years with rebates.
2. Passage 1: a resident and parent (first person, personal). Passage 2: a landscaper, a business owner with money at stake.
3. Passage 2. It gives specific costs and battery life. Passage 1 uses one personal story and “everyone I know,” an overgeneralization.
4. Complicate. Passage 2 accepts a ban as the goal but adds a cost and a limit: do it slowly, with help.

notes.say: This warm-up reviews last week: comparing two texts on the same topic. Give the student about a minute per question and ask for a reason with each answer. Remind them of the routine: read each passage alone, label who, claim, and purpose, then compare. Question 4 is the hardest; the landscaper does not simply disagree.
ask: Does the landscaper disagree with everything the resident says? (expected: no; the landscaper still supports a ban, just a slower one)
notes.answer: 1. P1: ban gas blowers. P2: phase in a ban over three years with rebates, because a sudden ban hurts small businesses. 2. P1: a resident and parent; P2: a landscaper, a business owner. 3. P2: specific, relevant numbers; P1 relies on one anecdote and the generalization “everyone I know.” 4. Complicate: P2 agrees with the goal but adds a cost and a limit.
notes.watch: If the student answers “disagree” on question 4, ask them to find the sentence where the landscaper says what the town should do. A phased-in ban is still a ban. Assuming opposing writers disagree about everything was one of last week's traps.

slides.title: What makes a complete sentence
slides.board:
Subject (who or what) + verb (action or state) + complete thought

ExampleStands alone?
Independent clauseThe bus arrived.Yes
Dependent clauseWhen the bus arrivedNo

Dependent clauses start with words like because, although, when, if, since, unless, while, which, who.

The “...and?” test: read it alone. If a listener would say “...and?”, it is not complete.

notes.say: Every complete sentence needs three things: a subject, a verb, and a complete thought. A group of words with a subject and a verb is a clause. If it can stand on its own, it is independent. If it starts with a word like because or when, it becomes dependent: it has a subject and a verb but leaves the reader hanging. Give the student the “...and?” test: read the words alone, as if you just walked into the room. Length does not decide it. “Stop.” is a complete sentence; a long phrase can still be a fragment.
ask: Is “Stop.” a complete sentence? (expected: yes; it is a command, and the subject you is understood)
What changes when you put because in front of “The bus arrived”? (expected: it becomes a dependent clause and cannot stand alone)
notes.watch: Many learners think long means complete and short means fragment. Keep returning to the three parts. Have them point to the subject and the verb, then run the “...and?” test.

slides.title: Sentence or fragment?
slides.board:
Label each one S (sentence) or F (fragment).

  1. When the clinic opens on Saturdays.
  2. Sign the form before you leave.
  3. The manager who hired me last spring.
  4. Working two jobs and still finding time to study.
steps: 1. F. When makes it a dependent clause. “When the clinic opens on Saturdays...and?”
2. S. A command. The subject you is understood; the verb is sign.
3. F. Subject: the manager. But hired belongs to “who hired me.” What did the manager do? No main verb.
4. F. An -ing word alone cannot be the main verb. Who is working? No subject, no main verb.

notes.say: Model the test out loud for each one: find the subject, find the main verb, then ask “...and?” Show that item 3 is the tricky one: it has a subject and a verb, but the verb belongs to the who clause, so the sentence never says what the manager did.
ask: How could you make item 3 a sentence? (expected: add a main verb, such as “The manager who hired me last spring retired.”)

slides.title: Three kinds of fragments, two fixes
slides.board:
FragmentExample
Dependent clause aloneBecause the system was down.
No subject or no main verbIncluding all part-time staff.
-ing or to phrase aloneHoping to finish by noon.

Fix 1 (most common on the GED): attach it to the sentence next to it.

Fix 2: add the missing subject or verb.

Comma rule: Because it rained, we left. · We left because it rained.

notes.say: Most fragments on the GED are pieces that broke off a neighboring sentence. The fastest repair is to glue the piece back on. Walk through the comma rule at the bottom: when a because clause comes first, put a comma after it; when it comes second, you usually need no comma. The second fix, adding what is missing, works too, but the GED menu usually offers the attaching version.
ask: Which fix would you use for “Including all part-time staff”? (expected: attach it, as in “The new rule covers everyone, including all part-time staff.”)
notes.watch: Learners sometimes “fix” a fragment by adding a comma inside it (“Because, the system was down.”). A comma never turns a fragment into a sentence. Something has to be attached or added.

slides.title: Fixing a fragment
slides.board:
We are closing early on Friday. Because the electricians need to replace the main panel.

Find the fragment and fix it.
steps: Step 1. Test each group alone. “Because the electricians need to replace the main panel...and?” It is a dependent clause.
Step 2. Find its partner. It tells why the office is closing early.
Step 3. Attach it: We are closing early on Friday because the electricians need to replace the main panel.
Step 4. Or flip it and add a comma: Because the electricians need to replace the main panel, we are closing early on Friday.

notes.say: Show each step slowly. The key move is step 2: decide which sentence the fragment belongs to. Here the because clause explains why the office is closing, so it attaches to the sentence before it. Then show the comma rule both ways.
ask: Why is there no comma in the step 3 version? (expected: the because clause comes second)

slides.title: Fragments in a notice
slides.board:
(1) The Riverside Food Pantry needs volunteers for its Saturday distribution. (2) Which runs from 9:00 a.m. to noon. (3) Volunteers should arrive by 8:45. (4) Bringing work gloves if you have them.

Which sentences are fragments? Fix each one.
steps: Sentences 1 and 3 are complete: pantry needs, volunteers should arrive.
Sentence 2 is a fragment: a which clause. Attach it with a comma: ...for its Saturday distribution, which runs from 9:00 a.m. to noon.
Sentence 4 is a fragment: an -ing phrase with no subject. Make it a command: Bring work gloves if you have them.

notes.say: Now the student leads. Ask them to test each sentence alone before you reveal anything. Sentence 4 is a good discussion point: you can fix it by attaching it or by turning it into a command.
ask: What word made sentence 2 a fragment? (expected: which)
Is sentence 3 complete even though it is short? (expected: yes; subject and verb, complete thought)
notes.answer: Fragments: 2 and 4. Fix 2 by attaching it to sentence 1 with a comma before which. Fix 4 by changing Bringing to Bring (a command) or by attaching it: “Volunteers should arrive by 8:45, bringing work gloves if they have them.”
notes.watch: If the student calls sentence 3 a fragment because it is short, go back to the three parts. Short is fine.

slides.title: Run-ons and comma splices
slides.board:
Run-on: two sentences, no punctuation. The store opens at nine it closes at six.

Comma splice: two sentences, only a comma. The store opens at nine, it closes at six.

Five repairsExample
Period...at nine. It closes...
Semicolon...at nine; it closes...
Comma + FANBOYS...at nine, and it closes...
; transition,...at nine; however, it stays open...
Subordinating wordAlthough it opens late, it...

FANBOYS: for, and, nor, but, or, yet, so

notes.say: A comma is not strong enough to hold two complete sentences together by itself. That is the whole rule behind comma splices. Write the five repairs on the board as a menu, and point out that four of them only change punctuation or add one word. The fourth repair is the one the GED loves to test: a transition like however needs a semicolon before it and a comma after it when it sits between two sentences.
ask: Name the seven FANBOYS words. (expected: for, and, nor, but, or, yet, so)
Is “The store opens at nine and closes at six.” a run-on? (expected: no; one subject, the store, with two verbs)
notes.watch: Learners often think any long sentence is a run-on. A run-on is about structure, not length. Have them find the subjects and verbs and count the independent clauses.

slides.title: One comma splice, five fixes
slides.board:
The printer is jammed, the reports will be late.

Is it correct? If not, fix it.
steps: Step 1. “The printer is jammed” stands alone. “The reports will be late” stands alone. Joined by only a comma: comma splice.
Step 2. Relationship: the jam causes the delay.
Step 3. Fixes: ...jammed. The reports... · ...jammed; the reports... · ...jammed, so the reports... · ...jammed; as a result, the reports... · Because the printer is jammed, the reports...
Trap: The printer is jammed, therefore, the reports will be late. is still a comma splice. Therefore is not a FANBOYS word.

notes.say: Model the full routine: check each side, name the relationship, then choose a repair that fits both the grammar and the logic. Finish with the trap in the last step; it is the most common splice on the test.
ask: Would “The printer is jammed, but the reports will be late” fix it? (expected: the punctuation is fine, but but shows contrast, and these ideas are cause and effect)

slides.title: Splice, run-on, or correct?
slides.board:
1. I called the office, nobody answered.
  2. The store opens at nine and closes at six.
  3. Rent is due on the first, however, the office accepts it until the fifth.
  4. The bus was late I missed the start of my shift.

Name each one, then fix the broken ones.
steps: 1. Comma splice. The ideas contrast: I called the office, but nobody answered.
2. Correct. One subject (the store) with two verbs (opens, closes). Not a run-on.
3. Comma splice with a transition: Rent is due on the first; however, the office accepts it until the fifth.
4. Run-on. Cause and effect: The bus was late, so I missed the start of my shift.

notes.say: Let the student name each sentence before revealing. Sentence 2 is there on purpose: it has one subject and two verbs, so it is correct. Sentence 3 is the however trap. For each fix, ask the student to name the relationship first.
ask: How many subjects does sentence 2 have? (expected: one, the store)
What punctuation goes before however in sentence 3? (expected: a semicolon, or a period)
notes.answer: 1. Comma splice; fix with , but (or a period or semicolon). 2. Correct. 3. Comma splice; fix with ; however, (or a period: “...on the first. However, the office...”). 4. Run-on; fix with , so (or Because the bus was late, I missed...).
notes.watch: If the student marks sentence 2 as a run-on, have them circle every subject. There is only one, so there is only one clause.

slides.title: Pick the joining word by the logic
slides.board:
RelationshipJoining wordsTransitions
Addingandin addition, also
Contrastbut, yet, although, whilehowever, instead, nevertheless
Cause / effectso, because, sincetherefore, as a result
Examplefor example, for instance
Timewhen, after, before, untilthen, afterward, finally
Conditionif, unlessotherwise

Coordination joins equal ideas (FANBOYS). Subordination makes one idea depend on the other (because, although).

notes.say: Transition and joining-word questions are really logic questions dressed up as grammar. Teach the routine: cover the choices, read the sentence before and the sentence after, and name the relationship in one word. Only then look at the menu. Point out that so and therefore mean nearly the same thing but are punctuated differently: so joins with a comma; therefore needs a semicolon or a period before it.
ask: Give two words that show contrast. (expected: any two of but, yet, although, however, instead, nevertheless)
What is the difference between so and therefore? (expected: same meaning; so can follow a comma, therefore cannot join sentences with a comma)

slides.title: Choosing a transition
slides.board:
The clinic extended its evening hours. [ ___ ], patients can now book appointments until 8:00 p.m.

However · As a result · For example · Instead
steps: Step 1. Name the relationship: longer hours cause later appointments. Cause and effect.
Step 2. Sort the choices: However and Instead = contrast. For example = example. As a result = effect.
Step 3. Answer: As a result. Read the pair aloud to confirm.

notes.say: Cover the choices first and name the relationship out loud. Then sort the choices into relationships before picking. This habit protects the student from choosing whatever sounds smooth.
ask: Why not For example? (expected: later appointments are a result of the change, not an example of it)

slides.title: Pick the joining word
slides.board:
1. [ ___ ] the forecast called for rain, the picnic went ahead.
    (Although · Because · Since · So)
  2. The bridge is closed for repairs. [ ___ ], drivers should use Route 9.
    (However · Therefore · For example · Similarly)
  3. Many jobs require a license. [ ___ ], forklift operators must pass a safety test.
    (For example · In contrast · As a result · Otherwise)
steps: 1. Rain was forecast, but the picnic happened anyway: contrast. Although.
2. The closed bridge causes the detour: result. Therefore.
3. Forklift operators are one case of jobs needing a license: example. For example.

notes.say: For each one, the student names the relationship first and then picks. Reveal one answer at a time and ask why each wrong choice fails.
ask: In item 1, why not Because? (expected: rain would not cause a picnic to go ahead; the ideas contrast)
notes.watch: On item 2, some students pick However because it is the most familiar transition. Ask: “Is the detour the opposite of the bridge being closed, or because of it?”

slides.title: Misplaced and dangling modifiers
slides.board:
Rule: put a describing word or phrase right next to the word it describes.

Misplaced: next to the wrong word.
She served sandwiches to the children on paper plates. (The children are on the plates?)

Dangling: an opening phrase with no correct doer after the comma.
Running to catch the bus, my phone fell in a puddle. (The phone was running?)

Check: the word right after the comma must be the one doing the action.

notes.say: A modifier is any word or phrase that describes. Misplaced modifiers sit next to the wrong word, so the sentence says something silly. Dangling modifiers usually open the sentence with an -ing or to phrase, and the word after the comma is not the one doing that action. Teach one question: “Who is doing the action in the opening phrase?” Then look right after the comma. If that is not the doer, the sentence is broken.
ask: Fix the plates sentence. (expected: “She served sandwiches on paper plates to the children.”)
Fix the bus sentence. (expected: “Running to catch the bus, I dropped my phone in a puddle.”)
notes.watch: Adding or removing a comma never fixes a modifier. Neither does moving the opening phrase to the end of the sentence. The right doer has to come right after the phrase, or the phrase needs its own subject.

slides.title: Fixing a dangling modifier
slides.board:
After reviewing your application, you have been selected for an interview.

What is wrong? Fix it two ways.
steps: Step 1. Who did the action in the opening phrase? The company reviewed the application.
Step 2. Who comes right after the comma? You. The sentence says the applicant did the reviewing. Dangling modifier.
Fix A (put the doer after the comma): After reviewing your application, we have selected you for an interview.
Fix B (give the phrase its own subject): After we reviewed your application, you were selected for an interview.

notes.say: This sentence comes from a real kind of business letter, and it sounds fine at first. Model the question: who reviewed the application? The company did. Then look right after the comma: you. The sentence says the applicant reviewed their own application.
ask: Would “You have been selected for an interview after reviewing your application” fix it? (expected: no; it still says you reviewed it)

slides.title: Who is doing it?
slides.board:
1. The customer returned the blender to the store that was broken.
  2. To apply for the job, a résumé must be uploaded by Friday.
  3. Freshly washed and folded, Rosa put the towels in the closet.

Name the error. Then fix it.
steps: 1. Misplaced. The blender was broken, not the store: The customer returned the broken blender to the store.
2. Dangling. A résumé cannot apply for a job: To apply for the job, you must upload a résumé by Friday.
3. Dangling. The towels were washed and folded, not Rosa: Rosa put the freshly washed and folded towels in the closet.

notes.say: Have the student ask the two questions on every sentence: what is being described, and what word is it next to? Reveal each fix only after the student proposes one.
ask: In sentence 2, who should come right after the comma? (expected: you, the person applying)
notes.answer: 1. Misplaced: “The customer returned the broken blender to the store.” 2. Dangling: “To apply for the job, you must upload a résumé by Friday.” 3. Dangling: “Rosa put the freshly washed and folded towels in the closet.”
notes.watch: On sentence 3, students may say “Rosa is fine, she is the one putting them away.” Point out that the opening phrase is washed and folded; Rosa was not washed and folded.

slides.title: Parallel structure
slides.board:
Items in a list or pair use the same form.

Not parallelParallel
reading, writing, and to speakreading, writing, and speaking
to cook, to clean, and laundryto cook, to clean, and to do laundry
She is smart, kind, and works hard.She is smart, kind, and hardworking.

Pairs: both...and · either...or · not only...but also. What follows each half must match.

notes.say: Parallel structure is about rhythm and balance. If the first item in a list is an -ing word, the others should be -ing words. If the first is a to verb, the others should be too. Teach the student to underline each item and look only at its first word. Pairs like not only...but also follow the same rule: what comes after not only must match what comes after but also.
ask: Make this parallel: “I like hiking, to swim, and bikes.” (expected: “I like hiking, swimming, and biking.”)
notes.watch: Some students match two items and leave the third. Have them check every item against the first.

slides.title: Making a list parallel
slides.board:
The job requires lifting boxes, to drive a forklift, and good communication skills.

Make the list parallel.
steps: Step 1. Underline the items: lifting boxes (-ing) · to drive a forklift (to verb) · good communication skills (noun phrase).
Step 2. Three different forms. Pick one, the first: -ing.
Step 3. Rewrite: The job requires lifting boxes, driving a forklift, and communicating clearly.
Step 4. Read it aloud. A parallel list has a steady beat.

notes.say: Underline each list item on the board in a different color. Seeing three different shapes side by side makes the problem obvious. Then choose one form, usually the first, and rewrite the others to match it.
ask: Could you make all three nouns instead? (expected: yes, for example “strength for lifting boxes, a forklift license, and good communication skills”; any one consistent form works)

slides.title: Your turn: fragments and splices
slides.board:
1. Fix: Our office will be closed Monday. In honor of Memorial Day.

2. Fix two different ways: Rent is due on the first, a late fee is added after the fifth.

3. Sentence or fragment? Although the store opens at nine.
steps: 1. Our office will be closed Monday in honor of Memorial Day. The phrase had no subject or verb, so attach it.
2. Any two: ...the first. A late fee... · ...the first; a late fee... · ...the first, and a late fee... · Although rent is due on the first, a late fee is not added until after the fifth.
3. Fragment. Although makes it dependent. Fix: Although the store opens at nine, staff arrive at eight.

notes.say: Start a three-minute timer and stay quiet while the student works. When time is up, have them read each answer aloud and name the error type before you reveal anything.
notes.answer: 1. Attach the phrase: “Our office will be closed Monday in honor of Memorial Day.” 2. Any two correct repairs: period, semicolon, comma + and, or a subordinating word. A comma with however is not correct. 3. Fragment; remove Although or add a main clause.
notes.watch: On problem 2, if the student writes “..., however, a late fee...,” stop and revisit the however trap before moving on.

slides.title: Your turn: joining ideas
slides.board:
1. The new schedule saves the company money. [However · For example · As a result], some employees dislike the early start.

2. Combine into one sentence that shows cause: The road flooded. The school bus took a detour.

3. Correct or not? The shop's sales doubled, so it hired two more workers.
steps: 1. However. A drawback contrasts with the benefit.
2. Because the road flooded, the school bus took a detour. (or The road flooded, so the school bus took a detour.)
3. Correct. Comma + so joins two sentences and shows the result.

notes.say: Three minutes on the clock. For each answer, the student must name the relationship, not just the word.
notes.answer: 1. However (contrast). 2. “Because the road flooded, the school bus took a detour.” or “The road flooded, so the school bus took a detour.” 3. Correct: comma + FANBOYS, and the logic is cause and effect.
notes.watch: If the student marks problem 3 as a comma splice, remind them that a comma plus a FANBOYS word is one of the five correct repairs.

slides.title: Your turn: modifiers and parallelism
slides.board:
1. Hanging in the closet, Marta found her uniform.

2. The class teaches budgeting, how to save, and investing.

3. To keep the lobby safe, wet floors should be mopped right away.

4. The new hire not only learned the register but also was training two others.

Name each error and fix it.
steps: 1. Dangling: Marta was not hanging. Marta found her uniform hanging in the closet.
2. Not parallel. The class teaches budgeting, saving, and investing.
3. Dangling: floors cannot keep a lobby safe. To keep the lobby safe, staff should mop wet floors right away.
4. Not parallel: learned vs. was training. ...not only learned the register but also trained two others.

notes.say: Four minutes. These mix the two skills on purpose, so the student has to diagnose before fixing. Ask for the error name first, then the fix.
notes.answer: 1. Dangling modifier: “Marta found her uniform hanging in the closet.” 2. Faulty parallelism: “budgeting, saving, and investing.” 3. Dangling modifier: “To keep the lobby safe, staff should mop wet floors right away.” 4. Faulty parallelism in a pair: “not only learned the register but also trained two others.”
notes.watch: Problem 4 is the hardest. If the student is stuck, have them underline what follows not only and what follows but also and compare the verb forms.

slides.title: GED question: joining two sentences
slides.board:
The cafeteria will close at 2:00 p.m. on Friday [ ▼ ] cleaning crew will deep-clean the kitchen.

Choose the option that correctly completes the sentence.

A. , a
B. ; however, a
C. , so a
D. a
steps: A: comma splice. Two complete sentences joined by only a comma.
D: run-on. No punctuation at all between two sentences.
B: punctuated correctly, but however shows contrast. Closing early and cleaning do not contrast.
C is correct: comma + so joins the sentences, and the closing happens so the crew can clean (cause and result).

notes.say: This is the real format: a menu in the middle of a sentence, choices that differ by a mark or a word. Have the student read the whole sentence with each choice in place. Two of the choices are grammar errors; one is grammatically fine but says the wrong thing.
ask: Which choice is correct grammar but wrong logic? (expected: B)
notes.answer: C. A is a comma splice, D is a run-on, and B uses a contrast word where the ideas are cause and effect.

slides.title: GED question: which version is correct?
slides.board:
Which version of the sentence is correct?

A. Stored in the freezer, you can keep the soup for three months.
B. Stored in the freezer, the soup will keep for three months.
C. Stored in the freezer, three months is how long the soup will keep.
D. Stored in the freezer, it is possible to keep the soup for three months.
steps: What is stored in the freezer? The soup.
A: you comes after the comma. You are not stored in the freezer. Dangling.
C: three months comes after the comma. Time is not stored. Dangling.
D: it comes after the comma; it refers to nothing that can be stored. Dangling.
B is correct: the soup comes right after the phrase.

notes.say: Whole-sentence menus are common for modifier errors. Teach the shortcut: every choice opens the same way, so ask once who or what is stored in the freezer, then check the word right after the comma in each choice.
ask: What question do you ask first on every choice? (expected: what is stored in the freezer, and is that word right after the comma?)
notes.answer: B. In A, C, and D the word after the comma (you, three months, it) is not what was stored in the freezer.

slides.title: GED question: parallel structure
slides.board:
The training covers how to lift safely, reporting injuries, and the use of the eyewash station.

Which revision is correct?

A. The training covers how to lift safely, how to report injuries, and how to use the eyewash station.
B. The training covers lifting safely, how to report injuries, and using the eyewash station.
C. The training covers how to lift safely, reporting injuries, and to use the eyewash station.
D. The training covers lifting safely, reporting injuries, and the eyewash station is used.
steps: B: lifting · how to report · using. The middle item breaks the pattern.
C: how to lift · reporting · to use. Three different forms.
D: lifting · reporting · the eyewash station is used. The last item is a whole clause.
A is correct: how to lift · how to report · how to use. All three match.

notes.say: Have the student underline the three items in each choice and look only at the first word or two of each item. The correct choice is the one where all three start the same way.
ask: Could an all -ing version also be correct? (expected: yes, “lifting safely, reporting injuries, and using the eyewash station,” but that version is not offered)
notes.answer: A. Every item begins with how to. B and C mix forms, and D ends with a full clause.

slides.title: GED strategy: read the whole sentence with each choice
slides.board:
1. Read the whole sentence, and the one before it, before opening the menu.
  2. Put each choice into the sentence. Read from start to finish.
  3. Look closely: choices may differ by one comma, semicolon, or capital letter.
  4. Ask five questions: Complete? Joined correctly? Modifier next to its word? List parallel? Logic right?
  5. Correct and clear: the answer passes both tests.

Language items are quick points. Aim for about a minute each, and save time for the long reading passages.

notes.say: Drop-down choices are written to look almost the same, so reading the menu by itself is a trap. The student has to read each choice in place. The five questions on the board are this lesson in one list. Also talk about time: language items are among the fastest points on the RLA test, so the student should move through them steadily and bank time for reading passages and the extended response.
ask: Why read the sentence before the one with the menu? (expected: transitions and fragments often depend on the sentence before)

slides.title: Recap and next steps
slides.board:
• Sentence = subject + verb + complete thought. Fix fragments by attaching them.
  • A comma alone cannot join two sentences. Five repairs: . ; , FANBOYS ; transition, subordinating word.
  • Pick joining words and transitions by the logic first.
  • The word after an opening phrase must be the doer.
  • Lists and pairs: same form.

Next: Student Lesson → Practice Set A (Set B if under 80%) → Exit Check

notes.say: Ask the student to list the five comma splice repairs from memory before you reveal the recap. Then walk through what comes next: the Student Lesson reviews today step by step with checks, Practice Set A has 15 GED-style editing questions with the reasoning behind every wrong answer, and the Exit Check confirms they are ready for week 8, which finishes the language skills.
ask: Which of today's errors do you think you make most in your own writing? (expected: any honest answer; suggest they watch for it in the practice)

screens.title: What you will learn
screens.html:
On the GED Reasoning Through Language Arts test, some questions show you a draft, such as an email, a memo, a notice, or a letter, with drop-down menus in the middle of sentences. You choose the version that makes the sentence correct and clear. Many of these questions test sentence structure. In this lesson you will learn to:

  • tell a complete sentence from a fragment, and fix fragments
  • fix run-ons and comma splices five different ways
  • join ideas with joining words and transitions that match the logic
  • fix misplaced and dangling modifiers
  • keep lists and pairs parallel

Work one screen at a time. Most screens end with a check question. You must answer it before you move on, and if you miss it, you will see exactly why that answer is wrong. The same skills will make your own writing, including your GED extended response, clearer.

screens.title: What makes a complete sentence
screens.html:
Every complete sentence has three parts:

a subject (who or what) + a verb (the action or state) + a complete thought

Use the “...and?” test. Read the words alone, out loud, as if someone just walked into the room. If that listener would say “...and?” or “...what about it?”, the thought is not complete.

Length does not decide it. “Stop.” is a complete sentence: it is a command, and the subject you is understood. “The new manager from the downtown office” is not a sentence, even though it is longer. It names someone but never says what that person did.

Also watch for -ing words. “Working two jobs” has no subject and no main verb. An -ing word needs a helper (is working, was working) before it can be the main verb.

check.prompt: Which of these is a complete sentence?
check.hint: Check each one for a subject, a verb, and a complete thought. Remember that commands have an understood subject.
check.explain: “Stop at the front desk before your appointment” is a command. The subject you is understood, stop is the verb, and the thought is complete. The Because choice is the most tempting because it is long and has a subject and a verb, but Because makes it depend on another idea that never comes.
options: Stop at the front desk before your appointment.
The new clerk from the downtown branch office.
Because the elevator is being repaired this week.
Hoping to finish the weekly inventory before noon.
why: This names a person but never says what the clerk did or is. It has a subject but no verb, so it is a fragment.
This has a subject and a verb, but Because makes it a dependent clause. It leaves the reader asking “...and?”
An -ing word alone cannot be the main verb, and there is no subject. Who is hoping? It is a fragment.

screens.title: Independent and dependent clauses
screens.html:
A clause is a group of words with a subject and a verb.

  • An independent clause can stand alone as a sentence: The bus arrived.
  • A dependent clause starts with a word that makes it lean on another idea: When the bus arrived. It cannot stand alone.

Words that start dependent clauses include because, although, even though, when, while, if, unless, since, after, before, until, which, and who. Put one of these words in front of a complete sentence and it stops being complete:

CompleteNow a fragment
The payment arrived.Unless the payment arrived.
The office closed early.Because the office closed early.

A dependent clause is fine when it is attached to an independent clause: When the bus arrived, we got on.

check.prompt:
This word group is a fragment:

Since the bus route changed in March.

Type the one word that makes it a fragment.
check.hint: Which word could you remove to leave a complete sentence?
check.explain: Since turns the clause into a dependent clause. Remove it and you get a complete sentence: “The bus route changed in March.” Or attach the clause to a main idea: “Since the bus route changed in March, I take an earlier bus.”

mistakes.why: Changed is the verb, and the clause needs it. The clause has a subject (the bus route) and a verb; what keeps it from standing alone is the word in front, Since.
The phrase in March just tells when. Without it, “Since the bus route changed” is still a fragment. The problem word is Since.

screens.title: Fragments and how to fix them
screens.html:
A fragment is a piece of a sentence punctuated as if it were whole. Watch for three kinds:

  • A dependent clause alone: Because the elevator is broken.
  • A phrase with no subject or no main verb: Including all weekend staff.
  • An -ing or to phrase alone: Hoping to finish before noon.

Fix 1: attach the fragment to the sentence next to it. This is the fix the GED offers most often.
Fix 2: add the missing subject or verb.

A comma or semicolon inside the fragment does not fix it. A semicolon must have a complete sentence on both sides.

example.prompt: Our office will be closed Thursday. Because the carpets are being replaced.
steps: “Because the carpets are being replaced” is a dependent clause. It cannot stand alone.
It explains why the office will be closed, so it belongs with the first sentence.
Attach it. When the because clause comes second, no comma is needed.
example.answer: Our office will be closed Thursday because the carpets are being replaced.

check.prompt:
Which revision correctly fixes the fragment?

The library offers free computer classes. Including a class on building a résumé.
check.hint: The second group has no subject or main verb. Which choice attaches it to the sentence it belongs to?
check.explain: “Including a class on building a résumé” has no subject and no main verb, so it is a fragment. It gives an example of the free classes, so attach it to that sentence with a comma: “The library offers free computer classes, including a class on building a résumé.” The semicolon version is tempting because it looks like a stronger join, but a semicolon needs a complete sentence on both sides.
options: The library offers free computer classes, including a class on building a résumé.
The library offers free computer classes. Including, a class on building a résumé.
The library offers free computer classes; including a class on building a résumé.
The library offers free computer classes. Including a class that helps build résumés.
why: Adding a comma inside the fragment does not fix it. “Including, a class...” still has no subject and no main verb.
A semicolon must join two complete sentences. “Including a class on building a résumé” is not one, so the semicolon is wrong.
This only rewords the end. The second group still starts with Including and still has no subject or main verb.

screens.title: Spotting a fragment in a paragraph
screens.html:
On the GED, a fragment is usually hiding in a paragraph of good sentences. It often sounds fine when you read quickly, because your mind connects it to the sentence before it. Slow down and read each sentence alone.

Fragments often begin with these words: Because, Although, When, Which, Who, Including, Such as, Especially, or an -ing word like Hoping or Leaving. A sentence that starts with one of these words is not always a fragment, but it is always worth checking. Ask: is there a main clause after the opening words?

When the doors open, line up by the gate. is complete: “line up by the gate” is the main clause.
When the doors open at nine. is a fragment: there is no main clause.

check.prompt: The paragraph below is from a draft notice. Click the sentence that is a fragment.
check.hint: Read each sentence alone. Which one starts with a word that makes it depend on the sentence before it?
check.explain: “Which gives working patients time to come in before their shifts” starts with Which, so it is a dependent clause. It describes the 7:00 a.m. opening but cannot stand alone. Fix it by attaching it: “The clinic will open at 7:00 a.m. on weekdays, which gives working patients time to come in before their shifts.” Every other sentence has a subject, a verb, and a complete thought.
spans: The Parkside Clinic is changing its hours in June.
The clinic will open at 7:00 a.m. on weekdays.
Walk-in visits will still be accepted until noon.
Which gives working patients time to come in before their shifts.
Saturday hours will stay the same.
check.why: The most common wrong click is the short last sentence, “Saturday hours will stay the same.” It is short, but it has a subject (hours), a verb (will stay), and a complete thought. The Which sentence is the one with no main clause.

screens.title: Run-ons and comma splices
screens.html:
Sometimes the problem is the opposite of a fragment: two complete sentences are jammed together.

  • A run-on joins two independent clauses with no punctuation: The store opens at nine it closes at six.
  • A comma splice joins them with only a comma: The store opens at nine, it closes at six.

Both are errors, because a comma by itself is not strong enough to hold two sentences together.

Not a run-on: The store opens at nine and closes at six. There is one subject (the store) with two verbs. Only one clause, so nothing is wrong.

Run-ons are about structure, not length. A long sentence can be correct; a short one can be a comma splice.

check.prompt: Drag each sentence into the correct category.
check.hint: For each sentence, count the subjects. Two subjects with two verbs means two clauses; then check what joins them.
check.explain:
Comma splices: “The bus was late, I missed my class” and “The store opens at nine, it closes at six” each join two complete sentences with only a comma.

Run-on: “The bus was late I missed my class” has no punctuation between the two sentences.

Correct: the so sentence uses a comma plus a joining word; the because sentence makes one clause dependent; and “opens at nine and closes at six” has only one subject, so it is a single clause.
choices: The bus was late, I missed my class.
The bus was late I missed my class.
The bus was late, so I missed my class.
I missed my class because the bus was late.
The store opens at nine, it closes at six.
The store opens at nine and closes at six.
check.why: The most common mistake is putting “The store opens at nine and closes at six” under Run-on. It has only one subject with two verbs, so it is one clause and is correct. Another common slip is calling the so sentence a comma splice; a comma plus a FANBOYS word is a correct join.

screens.title: Five ways to fix a run-on or comma splice
screens.html:
RepairExample
1. PeriodThe store opens at nine. It closes at six.
2. SemicolonThe store opens at nine; it closes at six.
3. Comma + FANBOYSThe store opens at nine, and it closes at six.
4. Semicolon + transition + commaThe store opens late; however, it stays open until ten.
5. Subordinating wordAlthough the store opens late, it stays open until ten.

FANBOYS are the seven coordinating conjunctions: for, and, nor, but, or, yet, so. After a semicolon, the next word stays lowercase unless it is a name.

example.prompt: My shift ended at five, I stayed to help close the register.
steps: Both sides can stand alone, and only a comma joins them: comma splice.
The ideas contrast: the shift was over, but the writer stayed anyway.
Choose a repair that also shows contrast: comma + but, or Although.
example.answer: My shift ended at five, but I stayed to help close the register. Also correct: Although my shift ended at five, I stayed to help close the register.

check.prompt:
Choose the option that correctly completes each sentence.

1. The library closes at six on Fridays{{0}} book drop stays open all night.

2. Rent is due on the first of the month{{1}} late fee is added after the fifth.
check.hint: Each sentence has two complete thoughts. Which choices give you one of the five correct repairs, with correct capital letters?
check.explain:
Sentence 1. The two ideas contrast (closed vs. open all night), and a comma plus but joins them correctly: “..., but the book drop stays open all night.”

Sentence 2. A semicolon can join two closely related complete sentences: “...first of the month; a late fee is added after the fifth.” The next word stays lowercase.

why: This is a comma splice. “The library closes at six on Fridays” and “the book drop stays open all night” are both complete sentences, and a comma alone cannot join them.
With no punctuation, the two sentences run together. That is a run-on.
But is right, but it does not take a capital letter in the middle of a sentence.
Both sides are complete sentences, so a comma alone makes a comma splice.
No punctuation between two complete sentences makes a run-on.
The semicolon is right, but the word after a semicolon stays lowercase.

screens.title: The however trap
screens.html:
Words like however, therefore, also, then, instead, as a result, and for example are transitions. They show how ideas connect, but they are not joining words. They cannot join two sentences with commas alone.

WrongRight
It rained, however, the game went on.It rained; however, the game went on.
We were short-staffed, therefore, we closed early.We were short-staffed. Therefore, we closed early.

The pattern between two sentences is semicolon, transition, comma (or a period and a capital letter). Compare: so is a FANBOYS word, so We were short-staffed, so we closed early is correct.

A transition inside one clause just gets commas: The manager, however, disagreed. That is fine because there is only one sentence.

check.hint: Are there two complete sentences here? If so, what punctuation must come before however?
check.explain: “It rained all morning” and “the game went on as planned” are both complete sentences. When however sits between them, use the pattern semicolon, transition, comma: “It rained all morning; however, the game went on as planned.” The version with two commas looks normal, which is why it is the most common wrong choice, but it is a comma splice.
options: It rained all morning; however, the game went on as planned.
It rained all morning, however, the game went on as planned.
It rained all morning however the game went on as planned.
It rained all morning; however the game, went on as planned.
why: This is a comma splice. However is a transition, not a joining word, so commas alone cannot join the two sentences.
With no punctuation between the two sentences, this is a run-on.
The semicolon is right, but the comma belongs after however, not between the subject the game and its verb.

screens.title: Coordination and subordination
screens.html:
When you join two ideas, the joining word must show how they are related.

  • Coordination joins two equal ideas with a comma and a FANBOYS word: The bus was late, so I missed my class.
  • Subordination makes one idea depend on the other with a subordinating word: Because the bus was late, I missed my class.
RelationshipJoining words
Addingand
Contrastbut, yet, although, even though, while
Cause and effectso, because, since
Timewhen, after, before, once, until
Conditionif, unless
Choiceor, nor

A sentence can be punctuated perfectly and still be wrong because the joining word says the wrong thing. Always check the logic.

check.prompt:
Choose the joining word that shows the right relationship.

1. {{0}} the forecast called for heavy rain, the outdoor job fair moved into the gym.

2. The library building is closed on Sundays{{1}} its online catalog is available every day.
check.hint: For each sentence, name the relationship in one word (cause, contrast, time, condition) before you look at the choices.
check.explain:
Sentence 1. The rain forecast caused the move indoors, so the word must show cause: Because.

Sentence 2. The building is closed on Sundays, but the catalog is always available: the two ideas contrast, so , but fits. All four choices are punctuated correctly; only the logic decides.

why: Although shows contrast. Moving indoors is what you would expect when rain is forecast, so the ideas are cause and effect.
Unless sets a condition and reverses the meaning: the fair would move only if rain were not forecast.
Until shows time (up to a point). The forecast did not last until the fair moved; it caused the move.
So shows result. The building being closed on Sundays does not cause the online catalog to be available; the point is the contrast between closed and available.
Or offers a choice between two things. The sentence is not offering a choice between the closed building and the catalog.
For means “because.” The building is not closed on Sundays because the catalog is available every day.

screens.title: Transitions between sentences
screens.html:
Transitions connect one sentence to the next. GED transition questions are really logic questions.

RelationshipTransitions
Addingin addition, also, furthermore
Contrasthowever, nevertheless, on the other hand, instead
Cause and effecttherefore, as a result, consequently
Examplefor example, for instance
Timethen, next, afterward, finally
Conditionotherwise

Cover, name, match. Cover the choices. Read the sentence before and the sentence after. Name the relationship in one word. Then pick the choice that matches.

example.prompt: The clinic extended its evening hours. [However / As a result / For example / Instead], patients can now book appointments until 8:00 p.m.
steps: Name the relationship: longer hours make later appointments possible. That is cause and effect.
Sort the choices: However and Instead show contrast; For example introduces an example; As a result shows effect.

check.prompt:
Choose the best transition for the blank.

The community college offers several free programs for adults. ___ its Tuesday night class helps learners prepare for the GED.
check.hint: Is the second sentence a contrast, a result, or one specific case of the first sentence?
check.explain: The first sentence makes a general statement (several free programs). The second names one specific program. A specific case of a general statement is an example, so For example, is correct. As a result is the most tempting choice because it is so common, but nothing here is caused by anything else.
why: However signals a contrast. The GED class does not go against the first sentence; it is one of the free programs.
As a result signals an effect. Offering free programs does not cause the Tuesday class; the class is one of those programs.
Otherwise means “if not.” The sentence does not describe what happens if the college does not offer programs.

screens.title: Combining sentences
screens.html:
Some GED questions ask for the most effective way to combine two sentences. The best choice does three things:

  1. It is punctuated correctly (no splice, no run-on, no fragment).
  2. Its joining word shows the true relationship between the ideas.
  3. It keeps the meaning of both sentences without adding or reversing anything.

Start by naming the relationship. Then cross out any choice with a punctuation error. Then cross out any choice whose joining word shows the wrong relationship.

example.prompt: Combine: The bridge on Route 9 is closed for repairs. Drivers must use the detour on Mill Road.
steps: Relationship: the closed bridge is the reason for the detour. Cause and effect.
Cause words: because, since, so, therefore, as a result.
example.answer: Because the bridge on Route 9 is closed for repairs, drivers must use the detour on Mill Road.

check.prompt:
Which is the most effective way to combine these sentences?

Our team finished the inventory two days early. The manager gave everyone Friday afternoon off.
check.hint: Why did the team get Friday afternoon off? Pick the choice whose joining word shows that relationship.
check.explain: Finishing early is the reason for the afternoon off, so the relationship is cause and effect. Because shows that and is punctuated correctly, with a comma after the opening clause. The Although version is punctuated correctly too, which makes it tempting, but its logic is wrong.
options: Because our team finished the inventory two days early, the manager gave everyone Friday afternoon off.
Although our team finished the inventory two days early, the manager gave everyone Friday afternoon off.
Our team finished the inventory two days early, the manager gave everyone Friday afternoon off.
Unless our team finished the inventory two days early, the manager gave everyone Friday afternoon off.
why: Although signals contrast, but a reward for finishing early is exactly what you would expect. The ideas are cause and effect.
This joins two complete sentences with only a comma, which is a comma splice.
Unless sets a condition that reverses the meaning: it says the team got the afternoon off only if it did not finish early.

screens.title: Misplaced modifiers
screens.html:
A modifier is a word or phrase that describes something. The rule is simple: put it right next to the word it describes. A misplaced modifier sits next to the wrong word, so the sentence says something the writer did not mean.

MisplacedFixed
The customer returned the blender to the store that was broken.The customer returned the broken blender to the store.
She served sandwiches to the children on paper plates.She served sandwiches on paper plates to the children.
We will mail a guide to every member printed in large type.We will mail a guide printed in large type to every member.

To check, ask: What is this phrase describing? Then make sure it sits right next to that word.

check.hint: What belonged to the neighbor? Find the choice where that phrase sits right next to that word.
check.explain: The wallet is what belonged to the neighbor, so “that belonged to her neighbor” must come right after wallet. Moving “in the parking lot” to the front clears the way: “In the parking lot, Dana found a wallet that belonged to her neighbor.” The next-door neighbor version is the most tempting because it sounds natural, but the describing clause sits next to parking lot.
options: Dana found a wallet in the parking lot that belonged to her next-door neighbor.
In the parking lot, Dana found a wallet that belonged to her neighbor.
Dana found a wallet that belonged to her neighbor's parking lot.
Belonging to her neighbor, Dana found a wallet in the parking lot.
why: The phrase “that belonged to her next-door neighbor” sits next to parking lot, so the sentence says the lot belonged to the neighbor. It should sit next to wallet.
This changes the meaning: now the wallet belongs to a parking lot. The phrase about the neighbor should describe the wallet.
The opening phrase describes the word after the comma, Dana, so this says Dana belongs to her neighbor.

screens.title: Dangling modifiers
screens.html:
A dangling modifier is usually an opening phrase, often with an -ing or to verb, that has no correct doer in the sentence.

Running to catch the bus, my phone fell in a puddle. The phone was not running.

Check: Ask who is doing the action in the opening phrase. The word right after the comma must be that doer.

Two ways to fix it:

  • Put the doer right after the comma: Running to catch the bus, I dropped my phone in a puddle.
  • Give the phrase its own subject: While I was running to catch the bus, my phone fell in a puddle.

Removing the comma or moving the phrase to the end does not fix it.

example.prompt: To apply for the job, a résumé must be uploaded by Friday.
steps: Who is applying? A person.
Who comes right after the comma? “a résumé.” A résumé cannot apply for a job. Dangling modifier.
example.answer: To apply for the job, you must upload a résumé by Friday.

check.prompt:
Which revision fixes the dangling modifier?

While cooking dinner, the smoke alarm went off.
check.hint: Who was cooking? Find the choice that puts a person in the sentence to do it.
check.explain: A smoke alarm cannot cook. The fix gives the opening phrase its own subject: “While I was cooking dinner, the smoke alarm went off.” Now it is clear who was cooking. Moving the phrase to the end is the most tempting wrong fix, but the sentence still has no person to do the cooking.
options: While I was cooking dinner, the smoke alarm went off.
While cooking dinner, the smoke alarm suddenly went off.
The smoke alarm went off loudly while cooking dinner.
While cooking dinner the smoke alarm went off loudly.
why: Adding suddenly changes nothing about who is cooking. The word after the comma is still the smoke alarm.
Moving the phrase to the end still attaches it to the subject, the smoke alarm, so the alarm is still the one cooking.
Removing the comma does not fix a modifier. The smoke alarm is still the only possible cook in the sentence.

screens.title: Parallel structure in lists
screens.html:
Items in a list must have the same grammatical form: all -ing words, all to verbs, all nouns, all past-tense verbs, or all clauses.

Not parallelParallel
reading, writing, and to speakreading, writing, and speaking
I received deliveries, checked invoices, and was stocking shelves.I received deliveries, checked invoices, and stocked shelves.
She is smart, kind, and works hard.She is smart, kind, and hardworking.

Method: underline each item. Look only at its first word or two. Make every item match the first one.

example.prompt: Before the interview, review the job posting, practicing your answers, and you should choose your outfit.
steps: List the items: review (command), practicing (-ing), you should choose (full clause). They do not match.
Match them to the first item, a command.
example.answer: Before the interview, review the job posting, practice your answers, and choose your outfit.

check.prompt:
A writer's draft says:

After work, Luis picks up his daughter, makes dinner, and checking her homework.

Type the one word that should replace checking to make the list parallel.
check.hint: Look at the verbs in the first two items. What form are they in?
check.explain: The first two items are picks up and makes: present-tense verbs that go with Luis. The third must match: “Luis picks up his daughter, makes dinner, and checks her homework.”

mistakes.why: Check does not match picks and makes. The other verbs end in -s because the subject is Luis; the third must too.
Checked is past tense, but picks and makes are present tense. All three verbs must match.
That is the word in the draft. Checking is an -ing form, but the other items are picks and makes.

screens.title: Parallel pairs
screens.html:
Some joining words come in pairs. Whatever follows the first half must match whatever follows the second half.

PairParallel example
both...andThe job is both challenging and rewarding.
either...orYou can either call the office or send an email.
neither...norThe form is neither signed nor dated.
not only...but alsoShe not only learned the register but also trained two new hires.

Not parallel: She not only learned the register but also was training two new hires. (learned vs. was training)

Comparisons work the same way: Walking to work is cheaper than driving (not “than to drive”).

check.prompt:
Choose the option that keeps each sentence parallel.

1. The new scheduling app is not only cheaper than the old system {{0}}.

2. To pay your bill, you can either use the online portal {{1}}.
check.hint: Look at the word right after not only and right after either. The second half must start the same way.
check.explain:
Sentence 1. not only cheaper ... but also easier to use: two adjectives, so the halves match.

Sentence 2. either use the online portal ... or pay at the front desk: two verbs in the same form.

options: but it is also easier to use
but also it is used more easily
why: After not only comes an adjective, cheaper. After but also this choice puts a whole clause, it is... The two halves do not match.
Not only must be paired with but also, not and also.
This puts a clause after but also and changes easier into an awkward passive. It does not match the adjective cheaper.

options: or pay at the front desk
or at the front desk you can pay
nor pay at the front desk
or paying at the front desk
why: After either comes a verb phrase, use the online portal. This half starts with a place and a new clause, so it does not match.
Either pairs with or. Nor goes with neither.
Paying is an -ing form, but the first half uses use. Both halves must match: use... pay...

screens.title: Putting it together: GED editing items
screens.html:
On the test, any of today's errors can appear in the same draft. Use this routine on every drop-down:

  1. Read the whole sentence, and the one before it, before opening the menu.
  2. Put each choice into the sentence and read it from start to finish.
  3. Look closely: choices may differ by only a comma, a semicolon, or a capital letter.
  4. Ask the five questions:
    • Is it a complete sentence?
    • Are two sentences joined correctly?
    • Does each modifier sit next to the word it describes?
    • Are lists and pairs parallel?
    • Does the joining word or transition fit the logic?

The right answer is both correct and clear.

check.prompt: Which two sentences are written correctly? Select two answers.
check.hint: Run the five questions on each sentence: complete? joined correctly? modifier in place? parallel? logic?
check.explain: The semicolon sentence correctly joins two complete sentences. The When you arrive sentence attaches a dependent clause to a command, and its two verbs (check, wait) match. Each of the others has one of today's errors: a dangling modifier, a comma splice, a list that is not parallel, and a fragment.
options: Bring a photo ID; you will need it to enter the building.
When you arrive, check in at the front desk and wait to be called.
Arriving a few minutes early, the waiting room may be crowded.
Parking is free on weekends, however, the lot fills quickly.
The exam covers reading, writing, and how to solve math problems.
Because the building has two entrances on Main Street.
why: Dangling modifier. The waiting room is not arriving early. The doer, you, must come after the comma.
Comma splice. However cannot join two sentences with commas; use a semicolon before it.
Not parallel. Reading and writing are -ing words, but how to solve math problems is not. Use math or solving math problems.
Fragment. Because makes this a dependent clause with no main clause.

screens.title: Summary
screens.html:
Here are the rules to carry into Practice:

  • A complete sentence has a subject, a verb, and a complete thought. Length does not decide it.
  • Fix a fragment by attaching it to the sentence next to it or by adding what is missing. A comma never fixes a fragment.
  • A run-on has no punctuation between two sentences; a comma splice has only a comma. Fix them with a period, a semicolon, a comma + FANBOYS, a semicolon + transition + comma, or a subordinating word.
  • However, therefore, and for example cannot join sentences with a comma.
  • Choose joining words and transitions by logic first: adding, contrast, cause and effect, example, time, or condition.
  • Put every modifier next to the word it describes. After an opening phrase, the word after the comma must be the doer.
  • Keep lists and pairs parallel.

Next: Practice Set A (15 questions). Score 80% or higher on first tries to master it; otherwise take Set B. Then take the Exit Check.

stimuli.title: Draft Email: Forklift Safety Training
stimuli.html:
To: All Warehouse Staff
From: Marcus Bell, Warehouse Operations Manager
Subject: New forklift safety training

(1) Starting the week of May 5, every employee who operates a forklift must complete a new safety training course. (2) Because the company is replacing all six of our older forklifts with electric models. (3) The electric forklifts are quieter and easier to steer, they also stop faster and handle differently with a full load.

(4) Each course will be taught by an instructor from the manufacturer. (5) The instructor will cover battery charging, daily inspections, and safe loading. (6) We will hand out a pocket guide to every operator printed on waterproof paper. (7) The course takes about four hours, lunch will be provided.
