items.prompt: The paragraph below is from a draft notice posted at a community pool. Click the sentence that is a fragment.
items.hint: Read each sentence alone. Which one has no subject and no main verb?
items.explain:
Step 1. Check each sentence for a subject, a verb, and a complete thought.

Step 2. “Including a new evening class for adults who are learning to swim” has no subject and no main verb. Including is an -ing word, which cannot be the main verb by itself. The words who are learning belong to a describing clause about the adults, not to a main clause. Read alone, it leaves you asking “...what is this class part of?” This is the fragment.

Step 3. Every other sentence has a subject and a verb: pool will open, lessons will begin, forms are, lifeguards will be. A writer could fix the fragment by attaching it to the swim lesson sentence: “Swim lessons for children and adults will begin the following week, including a new evening class for adults who are learning to swim.”
spans: The Lakeview Community Pool will open for the summer on Saturday, June 7.
Swim lessons for children and adults will begin the following week.
Registration forms are available at the front desk and on the city website.
Including a new evening class for adults who are learning to swim.
Lifeguards will be on duty during all open swim hours.
items.why: Some learners click the swim lessons sentence because it seems unfinished without the class details, but it has a subject (lessons) and a verb (will begin). The Including sentence is the fragment: the words who are learning belong to a describing clause, not to a main clause.

items.prompt: Which revision of sentence 2 corrects the error in the email?
items.hint: Read sentence 2 by itself. What word keeps it from being a complete thought?
items.explain:
Step 1. Sentence 2 begins with Because, which makes it a dependent clause. Read alone, it leaves the reader asking “...and so what?” It is a fragment.

Step 2. The fix must add an independent clause. “This training is needed because the company is replacing...” adds the main clause This training is needed and explains why. Correct.

Step 3. The other revisions only move or add commas or add a which clause. Each still begins with Because and has no main clause. A comma never turns a fragment into a sentence.
options: This training is needed because the company is replacing all six of our older forklifts with electric models.
Because the company is replacing all six of our older forklifts, with electric models.
Because, the company is replacing all six of our older forklifts with electric models.
Because the company, which is replacing all six of our older forklifts with new electric models from the manufacturer.
why: This still begins with Because and still has no main clause. Adding a comma in the middle only splits the dependent clause; it does not complete it.
A comma after Because changes nothing. The clause still depends on a main idea that never comes, so it is still a fragment.
Adding a which clause makes it worse: now the company has no verb at all, and the group still starts with Because.

items.prompt:
Read this draft email. Choose the option that correctly completes each sentence.

To: All Staff, Third Floor
From: Tanya Brooks, Office Coordinator
Subject: Fire drill on Wednesday

Hi everyone,

Our building will hold a fire drill on Wednesday at ten in the morning{{0}} will sound for about two minutes. Please leave your desk right away and walk down the east stairway to the north parking lot{{1}} your supervisor will take attendance. Thank you for taking the drill seriously{{2}} helps us make sure everyone knows the way out.

Tanya
items.hint: For each blank, ask whether the words after it could stand alone as a sentence. If they can, a comma alone is not enough. If they cannot, they must stay attached to the sentence before them.
items.explain:
Blank 1. “Our building will hold a fire drill on Wednesday at ten in the morning” and “the alarm will sound for about two minutes” are both independent clauses. A period with a capital letter makes two correct sentences: . The alarm.

Blank 2. “where your supervisor will take attendance” is a dependent clause that describes the parking lot. It cannot stand alone, so a period would create a fragment, and a semicolon must join two independent clauses. Attach it with a comma: , where.

Blank 3. “it helps us make sure everyone knows the way out” is an independent clause, so a comma alone is a splice and no punctuation is a run-on. A semicolon correctly joins two closely related sentences: ; it.

why: This is a comma splice. “Our building will hold a fire drill...” and “the alarm will sound...” are both complete sentences, and a comma alone cannot join them.
With no punctuation between two complete sentences, this is a run-on.
This is still a comma splice, and The should not be capitalized after a comma.
A period would leave “Where your supervisor will take attendance” standing alone. It is a dependent clause, so that creates a fragment.
A semicolon must join two complete sentences. “where your supervisor will take attendance” is a dependent clause, so it cannot follow a semicolon.
A period here creates a fragment, and a new sentence cannot start with a lowercase letter.
“It helps us make sure everyone knows the way out” is a complete sentence. A comma alone makes a comma splice.
No punctuation between two complete sentences makes a run-on.
This is still a comma splice, and It should not be capitalized after a comma.

items.prompt: Which revision of sentence 3 is correct?
items.hint: Sentence 3 has two complete thoughts. Which choice joins them with a comma plus one of the seven FANBOYS words?
items.explain:
Step 1. Sentence 3 contains two independent clauses: “The electric forklifts are quieter and easier to steer” and “they also stop faster and handle differently with a full load.” Joined with only a comma, they form a comma splice.

Step 2. A comma plus a coordinating conjunction (for, and, nor, but, or, yet, so) correctly joins two independent clauses. “..., but they also stop faster...” is correct, and but fits the meaning: the forklifts are easier in some ways, but operators must learn how they handle differently. Correct.

Step 3. The however version is the most tempting because however also shows contrast, but it cannot join two sentences with commas alone.
options: The electric forklifts are quieter and easier to steer, but they also stop faster and handle differently with a full load.
The electric forklifts are quieter and easier to steer they also stop faster and handle differently with a full load.
The electric forklifts are quieter and easier to steer, also they stop faster and handle differently with a full load.
The electric forklifts are quieter and easier to steer, however, they also stop faster and handle differently with a full load.
why: Removing the comma leaves two complete sentences with nothing between them. That is a run-on.
Also is not a joining word (not one of the FANBOYS), so a comma before it still leaves a comma splice.
However is a transition, not a joining word. With commas alone it is still a comma splice; it would need a semicolon before it.

items.prompt:
Read the draft article. Then choose the option that correctly completes each blank in these excerpts.

Sentence 3, blank (A): The program runs every Saturday from February 1 through April 12{{0}} appointments fill quickly, so residents should call early.

Sentence 6, blank (B): Volunteers can also check whether a family qualifies for the Earned Income Tax Credit{{1}} can be worth several thousand dollars for a working family.
items.hint: For (A), check that both the grammar and the logic work. For (B), decide whether the words after the blank can stand alone or must attach as a describing clause.
items.explain:
Blank (A). Both sides are complete sentences, so they need a correct join. The ideas contrast: the program runs for many weeks, but appointments still fill quickly. A comma plus but joins them and shows that contrast: , but. The for example choice is punctuated correctly, which makes it tempting, but its logic does not fit.

Blank (B). The words after the blank describe the tax credit. Attach them as a describing clause with a comma: , which. A period creates a fragment, a semicolon needs a complete sentence on both sides, and , it creates a comma splice.

why: This is a comma splice. Both sides are complete sentences, and a comma alone cannot join them.
However is a transition, not a joining word, so commas alone make this a comma splice.
The punctuation is correct, but the logic is wrong. Appointments filling quickly is not an example of the program running every Saturday; it is a contrast.
A semicolon must join two complete sentences. “which can be worth several thousand dollars” is a dependent clause.
“It can be worth several thousand dollars for a working family” is a complete sentence, so a comma alone makes a comma splice.
A period leaves “Which can be worth several thousand dollars for a working family” standing alone. It is a fragment.

items.prompt: Which revision of sentence 6 corrects the error in the email?
items.hint: What is actually printed on waterproof paper? Put that phrase right next to that word.
items.explain:
Step 1. In sentence 6, the phrase printed on waterproof paper comes right after every operator, so the sentence says the operators are printed on waterproof paper. This is a misplaced modifier.

Step 2. The guide is what is printed on waterproof paper. Moving the phrase next to pocket guide fixes it: “We will hand out a pocket guide printed on waterproof paper to every operator.” Correct.

Step 3. The versions that open with Printed on waterproof paper are tempting because the phrase is no longer next to operator in the middle, but now it describes the word right after the comma, and neither the operators nor we are printed on paper.
options: We will hand out a pocket guide printed on waterproof paper to every operator.
We will hand out to every operator printed on waterproof paper a pocket guide.
Printed on waterproof paper, every operator will receive a pocket guide.
Printed on waterproof paper, we will hand out a pocket guide to every operator.
why: The phrase printed on waterproof paper still sits right after every operator, so the operators are still the ones printed on paper.
An opening phrase describes the word right after the comma, every operator. This still says the operators are printed on waterproof paper. It is now a dangling modifier.
The word right after the comma is we, so this says the writers are printed on waterproof paper. Moving the phrase to the front does not fix it.

items.prompt:
Read this draft notice. Choose the option that correctly completes each sentence.

Gym Closing for Repairs

The gym at the Fairview Community Center will close for repairs from July 1 to July 21. The floor is being refinished, and the bleachers are being replaced. {{0}} all basketball and volleyball leagues will play at Fairview Middle School for those three weeks. Open gym hours will be canceled during the repairs. {{1}} the fitness room and the pool will stay open on their regular schedule. {{2}} the gym reopens on July 22, leagues will return to their usual times.
items.hint: For each blank, cover the choices and name the relationship between the sentence before and the sentence with the blank: result, contrast, example, or time.
items.explain:
Blank 1. The gym is closing, so the leagues must move. The move is an effect of the closing: As a result,.

Blank 2. The sentence before says something is canceled; this sentence says other spaces stay open. That is a contrast: However,.

Blank 3. The leagues return at the time the gym reopens. This is a time relationship, so When is correct.

why: However signals an opposite idea. The leagues moving is not the opposite of the gym closing; it is caused by it.
The leagues moving is not an example of the floor being refinished or the bleachers being replaced. It is a result of the closing.
In contrast signals an opposite idea. The leagues move because the gym is closed.
Similarly means the same thing is happening. But open gym is canceled while the fitness room and pool stay open: different, not similar.
Therefore signals a result. Canceling open gym does not cause the pool and fitness room to stay open.
For instance introduces an example. The fitness room staying open is not an example of open gym being canceled.
Although signals contrast, but the gym reopening and the leagues returning go together; there is nothing surprising to contrast.
Unless would mean the leagues return only if the gym does not reopen, which reverses the meaning.
Even though signals contrast, like although. The leagues return because of the reopening, not in spite of it.

items.prompt:
Read the draft article. Then choose the option that correctly completes each blank in these excerpts.

Sentence 9, blank (C): To get ready for your appointment, gather your W-2 forms, find your Social Security cards, and {{0}}.

Sentence 10, blank (D): {{1}}
items.hint: For (C), look at the first word of each item in the list. For (D), ask who signs in at the front desk.
items.explain:
Blank (C). The list is gather..., find..., and ___. The first two items are commands, so the third must be one too: bring a photo ID.

Blank (D). The resident signs in, not the volunteer. Giving the opening clause its own subject fixes the problem: “After you sign in at the front desk, a volunteer will review your documents with you.” In the other versions, the phrase after signing in attaches to a volunteer or your documents.

options: a photo ID should be brought
you will need a photo ID
why: Bringing is an -ing form, but the first two items are commands: gather and find. The list is not parallel.
This is a whole clause in the passive voice. It does not match the commands gather and find.
This adds a new subject and verb, you will need, so the third item no longer matches the first two.

options: After you sign in at the front desk, a volunteer will review your documents with you.
After signing in at the front desk, a volunteer will review your documents with you.
After signing in at the front desk, your documents will be reviewed with a volunteer.
A volunteer will review your documents with you after signing in at the front desk.
why: The word after the comma is a volunteer, so this says the volunteer signs in. The person who signs in is the resident. Dangling modifier.
The word after the comma is your documents. Documents cannot sign in. Dangling modifier.
Moving the phrase to the end does not fix it. It still attaches to the subject, a volunteer, so the sentence still says the volunteer signs in.

items.prompt:
Sentence 7 of the draft article is a fragment:

Because the library has only twelve trained volunteers.

Type the one word you could delete to make sentence 7 a complete sentence.
items.hint: Which word makes the clause depend on another idea?
items.explain: Because turns the clause into a dependent clause, so it cannot stand alone. Delete it and you get a complete sentence: “The library has only twelve trained volunteers.” (Another good fix is to attach it to sentence 8: “Because the library has only twelve trained volunteers, each Saturday is limited to forty appointments.”)

mistakes.why: Deleting only leaves “Because the library has twelve trained volunteers.” It still starts with Because, so it is still a fragment.
Has is the verb. Deleting it removes the verb and leaves the group even less complete. The problem is the word that starts the clause.
Trained just describes the volunteers. Deleting it leaves “Because the library has only twelve volunteers,” which is still a fragment.

items.prompt: Sentence 7 of the email is a comma splice. Which two revisions correct it? Select two answers.
items.hint: Which choices use one of the five correct repairs: a period, a semicolon, a comma plus a FANBOYS word, a semicolon plus a transition and comma, or a subordinating word?
items.explain: “The course takes about four hours” and “lunch will be provided” are both complete sentences. Two of the five repairs appear here: a semicolon, and a comma plus and. The however version is the most tempting, but it is still a comma splice; it would need a semicolon before however, and the ideas do not contrast anyway.
options: The course takes about four hours; lunch will be provided.
The course takes about four hours, and lunch will be provided.
The course takes about four hours, however, lunch will be provided.
The course takes about four hours lunch will be provided.
Taking about four hours, lunch will be provided.
why: However is a transition, not a joining word, so commas alone still make a comma splice. It also signals a contrast the sentence does not have.
Removing the comma leaves two sentences with no punctuation between them. That is a run-on.
This creates a dangling modifier. The opening phrase describes the word after the comma, so it says lunch takes about four hours.

items.prompt:
Read this draft cover letter. Choose the option that correctly completes each sentence.

Dear Hiring Manager:

I am applying for the shipping clerk position at Brightline Supply. {{0}} I have not worked in shipping before, I spent four years as a stock clerk at Delgado's Market. In that job, I received deliveries, checked invoices against orders, and {{1}}. My supervisor often asked me to train new employees on the store's inventory scanner.

{{2}} I would welcome the chance to discuss the position with you.

Sincerely,
Keisha Warren
items.hint: Blank 1: does the writer's lack of shipping experience cause her stock clerk job, or contrast with it? Blank 2: match the form of received and checked. Blank 3: who is eager to learn?
items.explain:
Blank 1. Not having shipping experience is a weakness; four years as a stock clerk is a related strength. The ideas contrast, so Although is correct.

Blank 2. The list is received deliveries, checked invoices..., and ___. The first two items are past-tense verbs, so the third must be too: kept the stockroom organized.

Blank 3. The opening phrase Eager to learn new systems describes the writer, so I must come right after the comma: “Eager to learn new systems, I am confident that I could quickly master your inventory software.”

why: Because shows cause. It would claim that her lack of shipping experience caused her to work at the market, which makes no sense.
Since here means “because,” so it makes the same cause-and-effect claim as Because.
So that shows purpose. She did not lack shipping experience in order to work as a stock clerk.
Keeping is an -ing form, but the first two items are past-tense verbs: received and checked.
This is a whole passive clause with its own subject. It does not match received and checked.
This adds a new subject, I, so the third item is a full clause instead of a verb like the first two.

options: Eager to learn new systems, your inventory software is something I could quickly master.
Eager to learn new systems, I am confident that I could quickly master your inventory software.
Eager to learn new systems, my confidence is that I could quickly master your inventory software.
Eager to learn new systems, it would be easy for me to master your inventory software.
why: The word after the comma is your inventory software. Software cannot be eager to learn. Dangling modifier.
The word after the comma is my confidence. Confidence cannot be eager to learn. Dangling modifier.
The word after the comma is it, which cannot be eager. The person who is eager must come right after the comma.

items.prompt:
Read this draft memo. Choose the option that correctly completes each sentence. Pay close attention to punctuation and capital letters.

To: All Front Desk Staff
From: Lena Ortiz, Office Manager
Subject: New visitor sign-in procedure

Beginning Monday, every visitor must sign in on the tablet at the front desk{{0}} sign-in sheets will no longer be used. The tablet prints a name badge that each visitor must wear at all times{{1}} who refuses a badge should not be allowed past the lobby. Contractors may enter work areas only with an escort. {{2}} Please contact me with any questions.
items.hint: Blanks 1 and 2 each join two complete sentences. Which punctuation can do that alone, and how is a word like therefore punctuated between two sentences? For blank 3, ask who signs in.
items.explain:
Blank 1. “every visitor must sign in on the tablet at the front desk” and “paper sign-in sheets will no longer be used” are both independent clauses. A semicolon joins them, and the word after it stays lowercase: ; paper.

Blank 2. Two independent clauses are joined with the transition therefore. The correct pattern is semicolon, transition, comma, with a lowercase therefore: ; therefore, anyone. The logic fits too: because visitors must wear badges at all times, anyone who refuses one stays in the lobby.

Blank 3. The contractors sign in. Giving the clause its own subject fixes it: “After contractors sign in, a staff member must walk them to the work area.”

why: Both sides are complete sentences, so a comma alone makes a comma splice.
No punctuation between two complete sentences makes a run-on.
This is still a comma splice, and Paper should not be capitalized after a comma.
Therefore is a transition, not a joining word. With commas alone, this is a comma splice.
The semicolon is right, but the word after a semicolon stays lowercase. Therefore should not be capitalized.
With no punctuation before therefore, the two sentences run together. That is a run-on.

options: After signing in, a staff member must walk contractors to the work area.
A staff member must walk contractors to the work area after signing in.
After contractors sign in, a staff member must walk them to the work area.
After signing in, the work area is where a staff member must walk contractors.
why: The word after the comma is a staff member, so this says the staff member signs in. The contractors are the ones signing in. Dangling modifier.
Moving the phrase to the end does not help. It still attaches to the subject, a staff member, so the staff member still seems to be the one signing in.
The word after the comma is the work area, which cannot sign in. Dangling modifier.

items.prompt: Which is the most effective way to combine sentences 12 and 13 of the draft article?
items.hint: Why are small business owners being referred to someone else? Choose the joining word that shows that relationship.
items.explain:
Step 1. Name the relationship. The volunteers cannot do business returns, so business owners are sent to someone who can. Sentence 12 is the cause; sentence 13 is the effect.

Step 2. The combination must show cause and effect and be punctuated correctly: “Because the volunteers are not trained to handle business returns, small business owners will be referred to a low-cost preparer.”

Step 3. The Although version is the most tempting because it is punctuated correctly, but it signals a contrast that is not there.
options: Because the volunteers are not trained to handle business returns, small business owners will be referred to a low-cost preparer.
Although the volunteers are not trained to handle business returns, small business owners will be referred to a low-cost preparer.
The volunteers are not trained to handle business returns, small business owners will be referred to a low-cost preparer.
Unless the volunteers are not trained to handle business returns, small business owners will be referred to a low-cost preparer.
why: Although signals contrast, but sending business owners elsewhere is exactly what you would expect if the volunteers cannot handle their returns. The ideas are cause and effect.
This joins two complete sentences with only a comma, which is a comma splice.
Unless sets a condition that reverses the meaning: it says owners are referred only if the volunteers are trained.

items.prompt: Drag each sentence into the category that describes it.
items.hint: For each sentence: Is there a main clause? If there are two, how are they joined? If it opens with a phrase, who comes right after the comma?
items.explain:
Correct: the Although sentence attaches its dependent clause to a main clause, and the semicolon sentence joins two complete sentences correctly.

Fragments: “Although the shop opens at nine on most weekdays” has no main clause; “Including the two new cashiers who started on Monday” has no subject or main verb.

Comma splice: “The shop opens at nine, the staff arrives at eight” joins two complete sentences with only a comma.

Dangling modifier: in “Opening the shop at nine, the alarm must be turned off first,” the word after the comma is the alarm, and an alarm cannot open the shop.
choices: Although the shop opens at nine, the staff arrives at eight.
Although the shop opens at nine on most weekdays.
The shop opens at nine, the staff arrives at eight.
Opening the shop at nine, the alarm must be turned off first.
The staff arrives at eight; the shop opens at nine.
Including the two new cashiers who started on Monday.
items.why: The most common mistake is putting “Although the shop opens at nine, the staff arrives at eight” under Fragment because it begins with Although. The dependent clause is attached to a main clause, the staff arrives at eight, so the sentence is correct.

items.prompt: Which is the best replacement for For example, at the beginning of sentence 15 of the draft article?
items.hint: Read sentences 14 and 15 together. Is sentence 15 an example of the limit, or a different option for the people who hit that limit?
items.explain:
Step 1. Name the relationship. Sentence 14 says residents who earned $65,000 or more cannot use the volunteer service. Sentence 15 tells them what they can do in its place. That is an alternative, not an example, so For example is wrong.

Step 2. Instead, signals one thing in place of another. Correct.

Step 3. In addition is the most tempting wrong choice because sentence 15 adds information, but it adds an alternative, not another point of the same kind.
why: Similarly means the second idea is like the first. Using the computer lab on your own is not like being turned away from the service; it is an alternative to it.
In other words introduces a restatement. Sentence 15 does not repeat sentence 14 in new words; it offers a different option.
In addition adds another point of the same kind. Sentence 14 states a limit, and sentence 15 does not add another limit; it offers a way around it.

items.prompt: The paragraph below is from a draft library notice. Click the sentence that is a fragment.
items.hint: Read each sentence alone. Which one has no subject and no verb?
items.explain:
Step 1. Check each sentence for a subject, a verb, and a complete thought.

Step 2. “Especially for jobs in health care, retail, and transportation” has no subject and no verb. It is a phrase that adds detail to the sentence before it. This is the fragment.

Step 3. The others are complete: library will hold, employers have signed up, recruiters will accept and hold, printing will be. Fix the fragment by attaching it: “Recruiters will accept résumés and hold short interviews on the spot, especially for jobs in health care, retail, and transportation.”
spans: The Glenwood Library will hold a free job fair on Tuesday, October 14.
More than twenty local employers have signed up.
Recruiters will accept résumés and hold short interviews on the spot.
Especially for jobs in health care, retail, and transportation.
Free résumé printing will be available at the front desk.
items.why: Some learners click the short sentence about employers because it seems too brief to be complete, but it has a subject (employers) and a verb (have signed up). The Especially sentence is the one with no subject or verb.

items.prompt:
Read this draft email. Choose the option that correctly completes each sentence.

To: All Tenants, Building C
From: Rob Delgado, Property Manager
Subject: Water shutoff on Thursday

Hello,

The water in Building C will be shut off on Thursday from 9:00 a.m. to 1:00 p.m.{{0}} will replace the main valve during that time. Please do not use the restrooms during the shutoff{{2}} will not flush until the water is back on.

Rob
items.hint: For each blank, ask whether the words after it could stand alone as a sentence. If they can, a comma alone is not enough. If they cannot, they must stay attached.
items.explain:
Blank 1. Both sides are complete sentences, so a period and a capital letter make two correct sentences: . Plumbers.

Blank 2. “where the cleaning staff will set up a table” is a dependent clause that describes the place by the mailboxes. Attach it with a comma: , where.

Blank 3. “they will not flush until the water is back on” is a complete sentence, closely related to the one before it. A semicolon joins them: ; they.

why: This is a comma splice. “The water... will be shut off...” and “plumbers will replace the main valve” are both complete sentences.
No punctuation between two complete sentences makes a run-on.
This is still a comma splice, and Plumbers should not be capitalized after a comma.
A period would leave “Where the cleaning staff will set up a table” standing alone. It is a dependent clause, so that creates a fragment.
A semicolon must join two complete sentences. “where the cleaning staff will set up a table” is a dependent clause.
A period here creates a fragment, and a new sentence cannot start with a lowercase letter.
“They will not flush until the water is back on” is a complete sentence. A comma alone makes a comma splice.
No punctuation between two complete sentences makes a run-on.
This is still a comma splice, and They should not be capitalized after a comma.

items.prompt: Which revision of sentence 10 of the letter is correct?
items.hint: Find the two complete thoughts in sentence 10. Which choice joins them with a comma plus a FANBOYS word?
items.explain: Sentence 10 joins two complete sentences, “Planting day is Saturday, April 12” and “we would love for your staff to join us,” with only a comma. That is a comma splice. Adding and after the comma joins them correctly: “Planting day is Saturday, April 12, and we would love for your staff to join us.” The therefore version is tempting because it adds a word, but therefore cannot join sentences with commas.
options: Planting day is Saturday, April 12, and we would love for your staff to join us.
Planting day is Saturday, April 12 we would love for your staff to join us.
Planting day is Saturday, April 12, therefore, we would love for your staff to join us.
Planting day, which is Saturday, April 12, we would love for your staff to join us.
why: Removing the comma leaves two complete sentences with nothing between them. That is a run-on.
Therefore is a transition, not a joining word, so commas alone still make a comma splice. It also claims a cause that is not there.
This turns “Planting day” into a subject with no verb of its own. The sentence starts one idea and never finishes it.

items.prompt:
Read the draft memo. Then choose the option that correctly completes each blank in these excerpts.

Sentence 2, blank (A): The surface lot will become a patient drop-off area{{0}} a covered walkway to the main entrance.

Sentence 3, blank (B): The garage has 600 spaces{{1}} employees will no longer have to drive in circles looking for a spot.
items.hint: For (A), decide whether the words after the blank can stand alone. For (B), check both the punctuation and the relationship between the ideas.
items.explain:
Blank (A). “including a covered walkway to the main entrance” is a phrase with no subject or main verb. Attach it with a comma: , including.

Blank (B). Both sides are complete sentences, and the second is a result of the first: plenty of spaces means no driving in circles. A comma plus so joins them and shows the result: , so. The for example choice is punctuated correctly, which makes it tempting, but its logic is wrong.

why: A period leaves “Including a covered walkway to the main entrance” standing alone. It has no subject or main verb, so it is a fragment.
A semicolon must join two complete sentences. “including a covered walkway...” is only a phrase.
“It includes a covered walkway to the main entrance” is a complete sentence, so a comma alone makes a comma splice.
Both sides are complete sentences, so a comma alone makes a comma splice.
Therefore is a transition, not a joining word, so commas alone make a comma splice.
The punctuation is correct, but the logic is wrong. Not having to drive in circles is a result of having 600 spaces, not an example of it.

items.prompt:
Read the draft memo. Then choose the option that correctly completes each blank in these excerpts.

Sentence 7, blank (C): To get your new parking pass, complete the online form, upload a photo of your driver's license, and {{0}}.

Sentence 8, blank (D): {{1}}
items.hint: For (C), look at the first word of each item in the list. For (D), ask who is parking in the garage.
items.explain:
Blank (C). The list is complete..., upload..., and ___. The first two items are commands, so the third must be one too: pick up the pass at the Security office.

Blank (D). The employee is the one parking in the garage, so you must come right after the comma: “Parking in the garage without a new pass, you may receive a ticket from Security.” In the other versions the word after the comma is a ticket, Security, or it.

options: pick up the pass at the Security office
picking up the pass at the Security office
the pass can be picked up at the Security office
you will pick up the pass at the Security office
why: Picking is an -ing form, but the first two items are commands: complete and upload.
This is a whole clause in the passive voice. It does not match the commands complete and upload.
This adds a new subject and verb, you will pick up, so the third item no longer matches the first two.

options: Parking in the garage without a new pass, you may receive a ticket from Security.
Parking in the garage without a new pass, a ticket may be issued to you by Security.
Parking in the garage without a new pass, Security may give you a ticket.
Parking in the garage without a new pass, it is likely that you will get a ticket.
why: The word after the comma is a ticket. A ticket does not park in the garage. Dangling modifier.
The word after the comma is Security, so this says Security is parking without a pass. Dangling modifier.
The word after the comma is it, which cannot park. The person parking must come right after the comma.

items.prompt: Which revision of sentence 4 of the letter corrects the error?
items.hint: Who was walking through the garden? That word must come right after the comma.
items.explain:
Step 1. Ask who did the action in the opening phrase. People were walking through the garden. In sentence 4, the words right after the comma are the broken fence and cracked hoses, so the sentence says the fence and hoses were walking. This is a dangling modifier.

Step 2. Put the walkers right after the phrase: “Walking through the garden last fall, our volunteers could not miss the broken fence and the cracked hoses.”

Step 3. The it was impossible for anyone version is tempting because it mentions people, but anyone comes too late; the word right after the comma is it.
options: Walking through the garden last fall, our volunteers could not miss the broken fence and the cracked hoses.
Walking through the garden last fall, it was impossible for anyone to miss the broken fence and the cracked hoses.
Walking through the garden last fall the broken fence and cracked hoses were hard to miss.
The broken fence and cracked hoses, walking through the garden last fall, were hard to miss.
why: The word after the comma is it, and it cannot walk. Adding “for anyone” later in the sentence does not put a walker right after the opening phrase.
Removing the comma does not change who is walking. The fence and hoses are still the only possible walkers.
Moving the phrase into the middle still attaches it to the broken fence and cracked hoses, so they are still the ones walking.

items.prompt:
Read this draft notice. Choose the option that correctly completes each sentence.

Route 12 Detour

Starting March 3, Route 12 buses will not stop on Elm Street while the city replaces the water lines under the road. {{0}} riders who usually board at Elm and Fifth should walk one block to the temporary stop on Oak Street. The detour will add about five minutes to each trip. {{1}} the times for all other stops on the route will not change. {{2}} the work on Elm Street is finished in late April, buses will return to their regular route.
items.hint: For each blank, cover the choices and name the relationship: result, contrast, example, or time.
items.explain:
Blank 1. The buses will skip Elm Street, so riders must walk to a new stop. That is a result: Therefore,.

Blank 2. One sentence says trips get longer; the next says other times stay the same. That is a contrast: However,.

Blank 3. Buses return at the point the work is finished. This is a time relationship: Once.

why: Walking to the Oak Street stop is not an example of the buses skipping Elm Street. It is what riders must do because of it.
However signals an opposite idea. Riders walking to a new stop is not the opposite of the stop being closed; it follows from it.
Similarly means the same thing is happening again. The second sentence tells riders what to do as a result; it does not describe a similar change.
As a result signals an effect. Adding five minutes does not cause the other stop times to stay the same.
For instance introduces an example. The unchanged stop times are not an example of the five-minute delay.
Similarly means the same thing is happening. But one trip gets longer while other times stay the same: different, not similar.
Unless would mean buses return only if the work is not finished, which reverses the meaning.
Although signals contrast, but buses returning when the work is done is exactly what you would expect.
Before would mean buses return while the work is still going on, which contradicts the first sentence.

items.prompt: Which revision of sentence 3 of the letter is correct?
items.hint: Look at the form of each of the three items in the list. Which choice makes all three match?
items.explain:
Step 1. Sentence 3 lists three purposes: to grow vegetables, to teach their children about plants, and for meeting their neighbors. The first two are to + verb; the third is for + -ing. The list is not parallel.

Step 2. Make the third item match the first two: “to grow..., to teach..., and to meet their neighbors.”

Step 3. The and meeting their neighbors version is the most tempting because it drops the for, but meeting still does not match.
options: Families use the plots to grow vegetables, teaching their children about plants, and to meet their neighbors.
Families use the plots growing vegetables, to teach their children about plants, and meeting their neighbors.
Families use the plots to grow vegetables, to teach their children about plants, and to meet their neighbors.
Families use the plots to grow vegetables, to teach their children about plants, and meeting their neighbors.
why: The middle item, teaching, is an -ing form, while the other two are to + verb. The list is still not parallel.
This mixes growing and meeting (-ing forms) with to teach. The list is still not parallel.
This fixes the for, but meeting is an -ing form and still does not match to grow and to teach.

items.prompt:
Sentence 5 of the draft memo is a fragment:

When the shuttle stops running at 11:00 p.m. each night.

Type the one word you could delete to make sentence 5 a complete sentence.
items.hint: Which word makes the clause depend on another idea?
items.explain: When turns the clause into a dependent clause, so it cannot stand alone. Delete it and you get a complete sentence: “The shuttle stops running at 11:00 p.m. each night.” (Another good fix is to attach it to a main clause: “When the shuttle stops running at 11:00 p.m., night-shift staff may call Security for an escort.”)

mistakes.why: Stops is the verb. Deleting it removes the verb and leaves the group even less complete. The problem is the word that starts the clause.
Deleting a word at the end only shortens the time phrase. “When the shuttle stops running at 11:00 p.m.” is still a fragment because it starts with When.
Deleting running leaves “When the shuttle stops at 11:00 p.m. each night,” which still starts with When and is still a fragment.

items.prompt: Sentence 12 of the letter is a comma splice. Which two revisions correct it? Select two answers.
items.hint: Which choices use one of the five correct repairs: a period, a semicolon, a comma plus a FANBOYS word, a semicolon plus a transition and comma, or a subordinating word?
items.explain: “Our volunteers will pick up the donation” and “you will not need to deliver anything” are both complete sentences. Two of the five repairs appear here: a semicolon, and a comma plus so, which also shows the result. The however version is the most tempting, but it is still a comma splice, and the ideas do not contrast.
options: Our volunteers will pick up the donation; you will not need to deliver anything.
Our volunteers will pick up the donation, so you will not need to deliver anything.
Our volunteers will pick up the donation, however, you will not need to deliver anything.
Our volunteers will pick up the donation you will not need to deliver anything.
Picking up the donation, you will not need to deliver anything.
why: However is a transition, not a joining word, so commas alone still make a comma splice. It also signals a contrast the sentence does not have.
Removing the comma leaves two sentences with no punctuation between them. That is a run-on.
This creates a dangling modifier. The opening phrase describes the word after the comma, so it says you will pick up the donation, the opposite of what the writer means.

items.prompt:
Read this draft letter. Choose the option that correctly completes each sentence.

Dear Ms. Patel:

I am writing to ask for a change to my work schedule at the Lakeside warehouse. {{0}} my daughter's day care now closes at 5:00 p.m., I can no longer work the 9:00 a.m. to 6:00 p.m. shift. In my two years on that shift, I have trained new pickers, covered extra shifts during the holidays, and {{1}}.

{{2}} I would be glad to discuss any option that works for the team.

Sincerely,
Andre Simmons
items.hint: Blank 1: does the day care's new closing time cause the problem or contrast with it? Blank 2: match the form of trained and covered. Blank 3: what has two open spots?
items.explain:
Blank 1. The day care's earlier closing is the reason the writer cannot work until 6:00, so the word must show cause: Because.

Blank 2. The list is (have) trained..., covered..., and ___. The third item must also be a past participle that works with have: kept my accuracy rate above 99 percent.

Blank 3. The early shift is what has two open spots, so the describing clause must sit right next to the early shift: “I would like to move to the early shift, which has two open spots.” In the other versions, the phrase describes the writer or the act of moving.

why: Although signals contrast, but the day care closing earlier is the reason the writer cannot work late. The ideas are cause and effect.
Unless would mean the writer cannot work the shift only if the day care does not close at 5:00, which reverses the meaning.
Even though signals contrast, like although. The earlier closing causes the problem; it does not contrast with it.

options: kept my accuracy rate above 99 percent
keeping my accuracy rate above 99 percent
my accuracy rate stayed above 99 percent
I was keeping my accuracy rate above 99 percent
why: Keeping is an -ing form, but the first two items are trained and covered (with have). The list is not parallel.
This is a whole clause with a new subject, my accuracy rate. It does not match trained and covered.
This adds a new subject and a different verb form, I was keeping, so the third item is a full clause instead of a verb like the first two.

options: I would like to move to the early shift, which has two open spots.
With two open spots, I would like to move to the early shift.
I would like to move with two open spots to the early shift.
Having two open spots, I would like to move to the early shift.
why: The opening phrase describes the word after the comma, I, so this says the writer has two open spots. The shift has the open spots.
The phrase with two open spots sits next to move, so it sounds as if the writer is moving while carrying two open spots. It should sit next to the early shift.
The opening phrase describes I, so this says the writer has two open spots. The shift is what has them.

items.prompt:
Read this draft memo. Choose the option that correctly completes each sentence. Pay close attention to punctuation and capital letters.

To: All Employees
From: Carla Nguyen, Human Resources
Subject: New key card system

Starting Monday, all employees must use their new key cards to enter the building{{0}} keys will no longer open the front doors. Each card records the time an employee enters{{1}} must never be lent to anyone else. Lost cards should be reported to Security right away. {{2}} Please contact Human Resources with any questions.
items.hint: Blanks 1 and 2 each join two complete sentences. How must a word like therefore be punctuated between two sentences? For blank 3, ask who reports the lost card.
items.explain:
Blank 1. “all employees must use their new key cards to enter the building” and “metal keys will no longer open the front doors” are both independent clauses. A semicolon joins them, and the next word stays lowercase: ; metal.

Blank 2. Two independent clauses are joined with the transition therefore, so use semicolon, transition, comma, with a lowercase therefore: ; therefore, cards. The logic fits: because the card records who enters, it must not be lent.

Blank 3. The employee reports the lost card. Giving the clause its own subject fixes it: “After an employee reports a lost card, Security will issue a new one within one day.”

why: Both sides are complete sentences, so a comma alone makes a comma splice.
No punctuation between two complete sentences makes a run-on.
This is still a comma splice, and Metal should not be capitalized after a comma.
Therefore is a transition, not a joining word. With commas alone, this is a comma splice.
The semicolon is right, but the word after a semicolon stays lowercase. Therefore should not be capitalized.
With no punctuation before therefore, the two sentences run together. That is a run-on.

options: After reporting a lost card, a new one will be issued within one day.
A new card will be issued within one day after reporting a lost card.
After an employee reports a lost card, Security will issue a new one within one day.
After reporting a lost card, Security will issue a new one within one day.
why: The words after the comma are a new one, so this says the new card reports the lost card. Dangling modifier.
Moving the phrase to the end does not help. Nobody in the sentence can do the reporting; the subject is a new card.
The word after the comma is Security, so this says Security reports the lost card. The employee does. Dangling modifier.

items.prompt: Which is the most effective way to combine sentences 5 and 6 of the letter?
items.hint: Decide how the two ideas are related. Does being in a low corner explain the flooding, contrast with it, or set a condition for it?
items.explain:
Step 1. Find the relationship. Water collects in low spots, so the plots flooded because they sit low. Sentence 5 states the cause; sentence 6 states the effect.

Step 2. The combination must show cause and effect and be punctuated correctly: “Several plots flooded after every heavy rain last year because they are in a low corner of the lot.” It also leads naturally into sentence 7, which describes the fix.

Step 3. The Although version is punctuated correctly, which makes it tempting, but its logic is wrong.
options: Several plots are in a low corner of the lot, they flooded after every heavy rain last year.
Although several plots are in a low corner of the lot, they flooded after every heavy rain last year.
Several plots flooded after every heavy rain last year because they are in a low corner of the lot.
Unless several plots are in a low corner of the lot, they flooded after every heavy rain last year.
why: This joins two complete sentences with only a comma, which is a comma splice.
Although signals contrast, but flooding is exactly what you would expect in a low spot. The ideas are cause and effect.
Unless sets up a condition that reverses the meaning: it says the plots flooded only if they were not in the low corner.

items.prompt: Drag each sentence into the category that describes it.
items.hint: For each sentence: Is there a main clause? If there are two, how are they joined? If it opens with a phrase, who comes right after the comma?
items.explain:
Correct: the When sentence attaches its dependent clause to a command, and the so sentence joins two complete sentences with a comma plus a FANBOYS word.

Fragments: “When the delivery truck arrives at the loading dock” has no main clause; “Which means the store will open thirty minutes late” is a which clause with nothing to attach to.

Comma splice: “The truck arrived late, the driver had a flat tire” joins two complete sentences with only a comma.

Dangling modifier: in “Unloading the truck quickly, two boxes fell off the cart,” the word after the comma is two boxes, and boxes cannot unload a truck.
choices: When the delivery truck arrives, sign for every box.
When the delivery truck arrives at the loading dock.
The truck arrived late, the driver had a flat tire.
Unloading the truck quickly, two boxes fell off the cart.
The driver had a flat tire, so the truck arrived late.
Which means the store will open thirty minutes late.
items.why: The most common mistake is putting “When the delivery truck arrives, sign for every box” under Fragment because it begins with When. The dependent clause is attached to a command, sign for every box, whose subject you is understood, so the sentence is correct.

items.prompt: Which is the best replacement for However, at the beginning of sentence 9 of the letter?
items.hint: Read sentences 8 and 9 together. What is the garden offering, and why?
items.explain:
Step 1. Name the relationship. Sentence 8 states what the garden is asking for. Sentence 9 states what the garden will give back: a sign thanking the store. That is an exchange, not a contrast, so However is the wrong transition.

Step 2. In return, signals something given back for something received. Correct.

Step 3. Instead is the most tempting wrong choice, but it would mean the garden is offering the sign rather than asking for supplies.
why: For example would make the sign an example of the supplies being requested. A thank-you sign is not soil, fencing, or hoses.
Instead signals a replacement. The garden is not offering a sign in place of its request; it still wants the supplies.
On the other hand signals contrast, just like However. Offering a sign does not go against asking for supplies.

items.prompt: The paragraph below is from a draft flyer. Click the sentence that is a comma splice.
items.explain: A comma splice joins two complete sentences with only a comma. “Nurses will check blood pressure” and “a dentist will offer free screenings” can each stand alone, so “Nurses will check blood pressure, a dentist will offer free screenings” is a comma splice. Fix: “Nurses will check blood pressure, and a dentist will offer free screenings.” The counselor sentence attaches a dependent who clause with a comma, which is correct.
spans: The Riverside Health Fair will be held on Saturday, October 4.
Free flu shots will be available for adults and children.
Nurses will check blood pressure, a dentist will offer free screenings.
Visitors who need health insurance can meet with a trained counselor, who will explain their options.
Parking is free in the north lot.
items.why: The most common wrong click is the sentence about the counselor, because it is long and has a comma. But the words after its comma, “who will explain their options,” cannot stand alone, so the comma is correct. The blood pressure sentence has a complete sentence on both sides of its comma.

items.prompt:
Read the draft notice. Choose the option that correctly completes blank (A) in sentence 2.

Six new computers will be added{{0}} the lab a total of eighteen stations.
items.explain: “giving the lab a total of eighteen stations” is an -ing phrase with no subject. It cannot stand alone, so it must attach to the sentence before it with a comma: “Six new computers will be added, giving the lab a total of eighteen stations.” The period version creates a fragment; the this gives version creates a comma splice.

why: A period leaves “Giving the lab a total of eighteen stations” standing alone. It has no subject and no main verb, so it is a fragment.
A semicolon must join two complete sentences. “giving the lab a total of eighteen stations” is only a phrase.
“This gives the lab a total of eighteen stations” is a complete sentence, so a comma alone makes a comma splice.

items.prompt: Which revision of sentence 3 of the notice is correct?
items.explain: Sentence 3 joins two complete sentences, “The lab used to be open only on weekday evenings” and “it will now be open on Saturday mornings too,” with the transition however and commas alone. That is a comma splice. The pattern between two sentences is semicolon, transition, comma: “...weekday evenings; however, it will now be open...” The version with the semicolon after however is the most tempting because it has the right marks, but in the wrong order.
options: The lab used to be open only on weekday evenings; however, it will now be open on Saturday mornings too.
The lab used to be open only on weekday evenings, however it will now be open on Saturday mornings too.
The lab used to be open only on weekday evenings however, it will now be open on Saturday mornings too.
The lab used to be open only on weekday evenings, however; it will now be open on Saturday mornings too.
why: Removing the second comma does not help. However is not a joining word, so a comma before it still makes a comma splice.
With no punctuation before however, the two sentences run together. That is a run-on.
The semicolon is in the wrong place. It must come before however, between the two sentences, with a comma after however.

items.prompt:
Read the draft notice. Choose the option that correctly completes blank (C) in sentence 6.

Many visitors do not have internet service at home{{0}} the lab is often the only place they can apply for jobs.
items.explain: Both sides are complete sentences, so they need a correct join. The relationship is cause and effect: because visitors have no internet at home, the lab is often their only option. Use semicolon, transition, comma with a result word: “...at home; therefore, the lab is often the only place they can apply for jobs.” The however and for example choices are punctuated correctly, which makes them tempting, but their logic is wrong.

why: Therefore is a transition, not a joining word, so commas alone make a comma splice.
The punctuation is correct, but however signals contrast. Having no internet at home is the reason the lab matters, not a contrast with it.
The punctuation is correct, but the lab being the only place to apply is not an example of having no internet at home. It is a result.

items.prompt: Which revision of sentence 7 of the notice corrects the error?
items.explain: In sentence 7, the word right after the opening phrase is a computer, so the sentence says the computer signs in at the front desk. That is a dangling modifier. The visitors sign in, so each visitor must come right after the comma: “After signing in at the front desk, each visitor will be assigned a computer.” The the staff will assign version is the most tempting because it puts people after the comma, but they are the wrong people.
options: After signing in at the front desk, each visitor will be assigned a computer.
After signing in at the front desk, the staff will assign each visitor a computer.
A computer will be assigned to each visitor after signing in at the front desk.
After signing in at the front desk a computer will be assigned to each visitor.
why: The word after the comma is the staff, so this says the staff signs in. The visitors are the ones signing in.
Moving the phrase to the end does not fix it. The phrase still attaches to the subject, a computer, so the computer still seems to sign in.
Removing the comma does not change anything. A computer is still right after the phrase, so the computer still signs in.

items.prompt:
Read the draft notice. Choose the option that correctly completes blank (B) in sentence 5.

Staff can help visitors set up email accounts, apply for jobs online, and {{0}}.
items.explain: The list is set up email accounts, apply for jobs online, and ___. Both items are base verbs that follow “help visitors,” so the third must match: “...and print documents.” The to print choice is tempting because “help visitors to print” sounds fine alone, but it breaks the pattern of the list.

why: Printing is an -ing form, but the first two items are base verbs: set up and apply.
This is a whole clause in the passive voice. It does not match set up and apply.
To print adds to, but the first two items are plain verbs without to: set up and apply.

items.prompt: Which is the best replacement for For example, at the beginning of sentence 9 of the notice?
items.explain: Sentence 8 sets a limit: one hour per computer. Sentence 9 says visitors who need more time can still get it by joining a waiting list. That is a contrast, not an example, so For example is wrong. However, signals the contrast. In fact is tempting because it often begins a sentence that adds detail, but it should push the earlier point further, not make an exception to it.
why: Similarly means the second idea is like the first. A way to get more time is not like a time limit; it is an exception to it.
In other words introduces a restatement. Sentence 9 does not repeat the one-hour limit; it offers a way around it.
In fact introduces something that strengthens the sentence before it. Sentence 9 softens the limit instead of strengthening it.

items.prompt:
Which two sentences correctly combine these sentences?

The training room is small. Classes are limited to ten people.

Select two answers.
items.explain: The small room is the cause and the class limit is the effect. Two choices show that with correct punctuation: a subordinating word (Because... ,) and a comma plus a FANBOYS word (, so). The Although and however versions are punctuated correctly but show the wrong relationship, and the comma-only version is a comma splice.
options: Because the training room is small, classes are limited to ten people.
The training room is small, so classes are limited to ten people.
The training room is small, classes are limited to ten people.
Although the training room is small, classes are limited to ten people.
The training room is small; however, classes are limited to ten people.
why: This joins two complete sentences with only a comma, which is a comma splice.
This is punctuated correctly, but Although signals contrast. A small room is the reason for the limit, not a contrast with it.
This is punctuated correctly, but however signals contrast. The limit is a result of the small room.

items.prompt: The paragraph below is from a draft newsletter. Click the sentence that is a comma splice.
items.explain: A comma splice joins two complete sentences with only a comma. “Childcare will be provided in Room 4” and “snacks will be served in the lobby” can each stand alone, so the childcare sentence is a comma splice. Fix: “Childcare will be provided in Room 4, and snacks will be served in the lobby.” The stories sentence attaches a dependent which clause with a comma, which is correct. “Everyone is welcome” is short but complete.
spans: The Northgate Adult Learning Center will hold an open house on Thursday, May 8.
Visitors can tour the classrooms and meet the teachers.
Students who finished the GED this year will share their stories, which many visitors find inspiring.
Childcare will be provided in Room 4, snacks will be served in the lobby.
Everyone is welcome.
items.why: The most common wrong click is the sentence about students sharing their stories, because it is long and has a comma. But “which many visitors find inspiring” cannot stand alone, so the comma is correct. The childcare sentence has a complete sentence on both sides of its comma.

items.prompt:
Read the draft email. Choose the option that correctly completes blank (A) in sentence 2.

Donation boxes will be placed in the lobby and the break room{{0}} employees pass by every day.
items.explain: “where employees pass by every day” is a dependent clause that describes the lobby and break room. It cannot stand alone, so attach it with a comma: “...in the lobby and the break room, where employees pass by every day.” A period creates a fragment, and a semicolon needs a complete sentence on both sides.

why: A period leaves “Where employees pass by every day” standing alone. It is a dependent clause, so it is a fragment.
A semicolon must join two complete sentences. “where employees pass by every day” is a dependent clause.
A period here creates a fragment, and a new sentence cannot start with a lowercase letter.

items.prompt: Which revision of sentence 3 of the email is correct?
items.explain: Sentence 3 joins two complete sentences, “Last year we collected 140 coats” and “the shelter says the need is even greater this year,” with however and commas alone. That is a comma splice. The pattern between two sentences is semicolon, transition, comma: “...140 coats; however, the shelter says...” The version with the semicolon after however is the most tempting because it has the right marks, but in the wrong order.
options: Last year we collected 140 coats; however, the shelter says the need is even greater this year.
Last year we collected 140 coats, however the shelter says the need is even greater this year.
Last year we collected 140 coats however, the shelter says the need is even greater this year.
Last year we collected 140 coats, however; the shelter says the need is even greater this year.
why: Removing the second comma does not help. However is not a joining word, so a comma before it still makes a comma splice.
With no punctuation before however, the two sentences run together. That is a run-on.
The semicolon is in the wrong place. It must come before however, between the two sentences, with a comma after however.

items.prompt:
Read the draft email. Choose the option that correctly completes blank (C) in sentence 6.

Many families at the shelter walk to work and school{{0}} a warm coat is a necessity, not a luxury.
items.explain: Both sides are complete sentences, and the relationship is cause and effect: because families walk everywhere, a warm coat is a necessity. Use semicolon, transition, comma with a result word: “...walk to work and school; as a result, a warm coat is a necessity, not a luxury.” The however and for instance choices are punctuated correctly but show the wrong relationship.

why: As a result is a transition, not a joining word, so commas alone make a comma splice.
The punctuation is correct, but however signals contrast. Walking everywhere is the reason a coat is a necessity, not a contrast with it.
The punctuation is correct, but a coat being a necessity is not an example of walking to work and school. It is a result.

items.prompt: Which revision of sentence 7 of the email corrects the error?
items.explain: In sentence 7, the word right after the opening phrase is the shelter, so the sentence says the shelter sorts the coats. The company's volunteers do the sorting, so they must come right after the comma: “After sorting the coats by size, our volunteers will deliver them to the shelter on December 20.” The they will be delivered version is tempting because it is short and smooth, but they refers to the coats.
options: After sorting the coats by size, our volunteers will deliver them to the shelter on December 20.
After sorting the coats by size, they will be delivered to the shelter on December 20.
The shelter will receive the coats on December 20 after sorting them by size.
After sorting the coats by size, December 20 is the date when the shelter will receive all of them.
why: The word after the comma is they, which means the coats. The coats cannot sort themselves. Dangling modifier.
Moving the phrase to the end does not fix it. It still attaches to the subject, the shelter, so the shelter still seems to do the sorting.
The words after the comma are December 20. A date cannot sort coats. Dangling modifier.

items.prompt:
Read the draft email. Choose the option that correctly completes blank (B) in sentence 5.

Coats should be clean, in good repair, and {{0}}.
items.explain: Each item in the list must fit after “Coats should be”: should be clean, should be in good repair, and should be free of large stains. The other choices add a new subject and verb or use an -ing form that does not fit after should be.

options: they should not have large stains
why: This adds a new subject and verb, they should not have, so the third item is a whole sentence while the first two are describing words.
This is a whole clause about stains, not a description of the coats. It does not match clean and in good repair.
Having is an -ing form. The first two items describe the coats after should be: clean, in good repair. “Coats should be having no large stains” does not work.

items.prompt: Which is the best replacement for However, at the beginning of sentence 9 of the email?
items.explain: Sentence 8 gives a reason: the shelter has no space for extra household items. Sentence 9 asks staff not to bring blankets, pillows, or shoes. The request follows from the reason, so the transition must show result: Therefore,. In contrast is the most tempting wrong choice because it is close to However, but there is no contrast here.
why: For example introduces an example. Not bringing blankets is not an example of the shelter lacking space; it is what follows from it.
In contrast signals an opposite idea, just like However. The request does not go against the lack of space; it is caused by it.
Similarly means the second idea is like the first. A request not to bring items is not similar to a lack of space; it is a result of it.

items.prompt:
Which two sentences correctly combine these sentences?

The bus was twenty minutes late. Several workers missed the start of their shift.

Select two answers.
items.explain: The late bus is the cause; missing the shift is the effect. Two choices show that with correct punctuation: a subordinating word (Because... ,) and a comma plus a FANBOYS word (, so). The Although and however versions are punctuated correctly but show the wrong relationship, and the comma-only version is a comma splice.
options: Because the bus was twenty minutes late, several workers missed the start of their shift.
The bus was twenty minutes late, so several workers missed the start of their shift.
The bus was twenty minutes late, several workers missed the start of their shift.
Although the bus was twenty minutes late, several workers missed the start of their shift.
The bus was twenty minutes late; however, several workers missed the start of their shift.
why: This joins two complete sentences with only a comma, which is a comma splice.
This is punctuated correctly, but Although signals contrast. The late bus is the reason the workers were late, not a contrast with it.
This is punctuated correctly, but however signals contrast. Missing the shift is a result of the late bus.

vocab.def: A group of words with a subject and a verb that expresses a complete thought and can stand alone as a sentence.
A group of words with a subject and a verb that cannot stand alone because it begins with a word such as because, although, when, or which.
vocab.example: because the meeting starts at noon

vocab.def: A piece of a sentence written as if it were complete; it is missing a subject, a verb, or a complete thought.
Two or more independent clauses joined with no punctuation or joining word.
vocab.example: The bus was late I missed my class.

vocab.def: Two independent clauses joined with only a comma.
vocab.example: The bus was late, I missed my class.

vocab.def: One of seven words that join equal ideas: for, and, nor, but, or, yet, so (FANBOYS). Use a comma before it when it joins two sentences.
vocab.example: The bus was late, so I missed my class.

vocab.def: A word that makes a clause dependent and shows its relationship to the main idea, such as because, although, when, if, or unless.
vocab.example: Because the bus was late, I missed my class.

vocab.def: Joining two ideas of equal importance, usually with a comma and a coordinating conjunction.
vocab.example: I applied for the job, and I got an interview.

vocab.def: Joining two ideas so that one depends on the other, using a subordinating conjunction to show the relationship.
vocab.example: Although I applied late, I got an interview.

vocab.def: A word or phrase that shows how one idea connects to the next, such as however, therefore, or for example.
vocab.example: Sales rose. As a result, the store hired more staff.

vocab.def: A word or phrase that describes another word in the sentence.
vocab.example: In the cracked window, cracked is a modifier.

vocab.def: A describing word or phrase placed next to the wrong word, so the sentence says something unintended.
vocab.example: She served sandwiches to the children on paper plates.

vocab.def: An opening describing phrase with no correct word in the sentence for it to describe.
vocab.example: Walking into the room, the lights went out.

vocab.def: Using the same grammatical form for items in a list or pair.
vocab.example: She likes hiking, biking, and swimming.

vocab.def: A group of words that has a subject and a verb. It may be independent (can stand alone) or dependent (cannot stand alone).
vocab.example: the office closed early (independent); because the office closed early (dependent)

notes:
Week 7 RLA Study Sheet: Sentence Structure

Complete sentence = 3 parts

  • Subject (who or what)
  • Verb (action or state)
  • Complete thought (no “...and?”)

Fragments

  • Dependent clause alone: Because it rained.
  • No subject or verb: Including all staff.
  • -ing or to phrase alone: Hoping to win.
  • Fix: attach to the next sentence or add what is missing.

Modifiers

  • Put the modifier next to the word it describes.
  • After an opening phrase, the word after the comma must be the doer.
  • Moving a comma does not fix a modifier.

Parallelism

  • Same form in lists and pairs: reading, writing, and speaking
  • Check pairs: both...and, either...or, not only...but also
  • Match each item to the first one.

Not a run-on

  • One subject, two verbs: The store opens at nine and closes at six.
  • Length does not make a run-on; structure does.

Five fixes for run-ons and comma splices

  1. Period: It rained. We stayed in.
  2. Semicolon: It rained; we stayed in.
  3. Comma + FANBOYS: It rained, so we stayed in.
  4. Semicolon + transition + comma: It rained; therefore, we stayed in.
  5. Subordinating word: Because it rained, we stayed in.

It rained, however, we went out. is still a comma splice.
